SciForge organizes the data, code, run records, results, evidence, and human review; the prediction capability comes from the external model you connect. The offline fixture, model adapter, and full continuous screenshots are not yet fully verified in the current version. This page publishes an implementable evaluation contract and operating boundaries; it does not present them as an "out-of-the-box built-in virtual cell model." Evaluation task The 2026 Virtual Cell Challenge task is zero-shot cross-cell-background prediction: the model receives unperturbed baseline cells and CRISPRi knockdown target genes, and predicts post-perturbation expression profiles in cell backgrounds it has not seen before. For the official description, see Arc Institute's task overview. This tutorial focuses on four common risks: - The model sees the sealed ground truth before prediction, causing data leakage - Data, weight, or environment drift makes results impossible to rerun - The output shape is valid but gene order, value type, or labels are wrong - Only the overall score is reported, hiding consistent failures on specific backgrounds or perturbations Choose a path first Path Purpose Ground truth and scoring External effects --- --- --- --- A. Offline reproduction demo After preparing offline data, walk through prediction, sealing, local scoring, and rerun Requires independently sealed validation data prepared in advance; this site does not yet provide a verified fixture, and it is not the official held-out ground truth No upload by default; a small local CPU slice works B. VCC 2026 online path Assemble the official inputs and run pre-submission checks Run the official CLI preflight locally; final scoring happens on the official server Downloads, sign-ins, uploads, and submissions each require separate confirmation The two paths can share the prediction artifact contract, but they must not mix ground truth or scoring claims. When you cannot determine the path, stop. Workspace boundaries in SciForge Start by inspecting the protocol, data, model, and existing runs in the SciForge Files panel; do not launch a full prediction right away. Figure 1: The Files panel is used to check the current workspace and key inputs; this feature screenshot is not a completed benchmark run. Suggested layout: text virtual-cell-benchmark/ ├── protocol/ │ ├── evaluation-plan.md │ ├── data-contract.yaml │ └── split-manifest.json ├── data/ │ ├── inputs/ │ └── sealed-reference/ Path A only ├── models/ │ ├── baseline/ │ └── external-adapter/ ├── scripts/ │ ├── validate_inputs.py │ ├── run_prediction.py │ ├── validate_prediction.py │ ├── evaluate_offline.py Path A only │ └── analyze_failures.py └── runs/<run-id / ├── run-manifest.json ├── environment-lock. ├── logs/ ├── predictions/ ├── validation/ ├── metrics/ ├── figures/ └── dossier/ run-manifest.json is the core index. At minimum it records the path type, input hashes, code commit, model and weight hashes, environment, device, random seed, prediction hash, command, return code, and timestamp. Official output contract snapshot As of 2026-09-04, the full submission contract given by the official VCC CLI documentation includes: Contract item Official requirement Local check --- ---: --- Perturbations × cells per condition × backgrounds 300 × 400 × 3 Exact counts per background and per perturbation Total predicted cells 360,000 Check obs row count and duplicate keys Gene dimension 18,533 Gene set, order, and uniqueness Values Raw, non-negative integer counts Reject log-normalized, scaled, or negative values Control cells Should not be included Scan for non-targeting control labels Local preflight vcc prep --dry-run Save the CLI version, command, return code, and full output The official bundle downloaded at run time and the VCC CLI documentation are the final authority; if the CLI disagrees with this page, stop and update the protocol. Full task prompt text Please organize a reproducible virtual cell perturbation prediction evaluation in the current workspace. Goal: use unperturbed baseline cells and the given knockdown target genes to generate post-perturbation expression predictions, and pin the data, model, environment, runs, and results into a reviewable evidence chain. First determine the path from the workspace: - Path A: offline reproduction fixture, where local scoring can run after predictions are sealed. - Path B: official VCC 2026, where locally you only run contract checks and vcc prep --dry-run. - If you cannot determine the path, stop. Do not guess or mix the two paths. Execution requirements: 1. Inspect Git, data, model code, weights, environment, and evaluation scripts in read-only mode. 2. Generate an input inventory and hash manifest, separating what the model can see from what it cannot. 3. Before the first prediction, fix the metrics, aggregation rules, and failure conditions. 4. Run a small-sample dry run first, and check shape, gene order, labels, value types, device, and random seed. 5. Once that passes, generate predictions and record the command, arguments, environment, resources, return code, and prediction hash. 6. For path A, only read the sealed fixture after predictions are sealed. 7. For path B, run only vcc prep --dry-run; stop and confirm before any download, sign-in, upload, or submission. 8. Break down error by background, target gene, expression range, and metric component; do not report only the overall score. 9. Add the protocol, inputs, runs, predictions, validation, metrics, failures, and limitations to the Evidence DAG. 10. Rerun from a clean environment and generate a Research Dossier. Without my confirmation, do not download weights, install dependencies, sign in to external services, submit compute jobs, or upload data. If the input contract, gene space, scoring path, or evaluation script cannot be verified, stop immediately. Execution phases 1. Pre-register the protocol Create evaluation-plan.md before the first prediction, and freeze the data split, primary metrics, auxiliary metrics, aggregation rules, model-visible content, and stop conditions. The file time and Git record must predate the prediction output. 2. Pin the model and environment Record the code commit, weight hashes, license, environment lockfile, device, and random seed. Do not silently download new weights, swap models, or change data preprocessing. When you need an external GPU or a lab cluster, you can submit the job to your own remote environment through the Terminal; the remote side still uses the same output contract. 3. Small-sample dry run Check on the smallest slice: - Input and output shape - Gene ID set and order - Perturbation and background labels - Cells per condition - Non-negative integer counts - Sparse storage and peak memory - Device, random seed, and return code If any hard contract check fails, do not proceed to the full prediction. 4. Run and seal predictions As soon as the full prediction finishes, compute its hash, write it into the run manifest, and put the logs, return code, and resource information under the same run-id . An original run must not be overwritten by a later rerun. 5A. Offline scoring Only after predictions are sealed may you open the sealed fixture and score with the frozen evaluation script. If the reference was read by the model or an analysis script before sealing, mark that run as invalid and start over in a new workspace. 5B. Official preflight Run vcc prep --dry-run with the current official CLI. Passing the preflight does not mean you have submitted. Any sign-in, packaged upload, or formal submission is an external operation: show the target, files, size, and purpose, and get user confirmation. Stratified analysis and evidence review Divide the results into at least four layers: 1. Contract layer : whether files, shape, gene order, count type, and labels are correct. 2. Metric layer : report every component, the overall score, and the aggregation rules. 3. Stratified layer : check performance by background, perturbation, expression strength, and gene abundance. 4. Biology layer : label pathway or cell-state interpretations as hypotheses, and do not write scores directly as mechanistic conclusions. Recommended figures include component metrics, a dot plot stratified by background, perturbation-level error ranking, a differential expression comparison of observed versus predicted values, and an in-depth profile of at least one failure condition. Finally, in SciForge, organize the protocol, inputs, runs, predictions, metrics, failure cases, and limitations into the research dossier. Figure 3: The Research Dossier aggregates the research narrative, versions, confidence, and limitations; continuous screenshots from the same benchmark session still need to be captured before the case is officially published. When you must stop Problem Risk Handling --- --- --- Background labels unknown or swapped Predictions that look valid on the wrong background Check against a fixed mapping and stop immediately Same gene set but a different order Distorted metrics Check both the set and the order before prediction and scoring Output is normalized or scaled values Violates the raw count contract Verify non-negativity, integer values, and provenance; stop on failure Wrong cell count per perturbation Condition weights shift Verify exact counts per background and per perturbation Environment or weight drift Reruns are not comparable Create a new run-id and produce a difference report Path B preparing an upload Data leaves the local machine Show the target and files, and wait for user confirmation Completion criteria These items are the acceptance criteria for a later integration run; this page does not provide proof of a completed prediction, scoring, and rerun. - Path A/B is clear and the two are not mixed - The protocol predates the first prediction - Input, code, weight, environment, and prediction hashes are all present - All hard contracts pass in the dry run - The overall score and stratified failures are reported together - Rerun differences are recorded and explained - No external upload or submission happened without confirmation Next: Remote resources and collaboration.

en.title: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence atlas
en.description: Review CRISPR perturbations, multimodal responses, figures, and evidence boundaries in SciForge.
en.body: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence atlas This case organizes CRISPR perturbation, target annotation, pathways, transcriptional response, protein response, and cell fitness into an inspectable cross-scale evidence chain. SciForge manages the workspace, execution process, figures, evidence, and human review. SciForge itself is not a virtual cell predictor. The five screenshots below come from the current SciForge development build and open real artifacts in a separate cross-scale-data-demo workspace. They verify the artifact browsing path, but they do not claim that the current version has already completed every rerun from the same session. Research question After a designated target gene is CRISPR-perturbed in a specific cell background, what changes in transcription, protein, pathways, and cell fitness? Which data and methods support each conclusion? The case must answer both "what did we get" and "what can we still not say." Differential expression, protein response, or phenotypic association cannot automatically be promoted to a causal mechanism; cross-layer missingness must also be preserved as a result. Final delivery package The following are the acceptance targets for one complete case run. The current screenshots already show data, figure, and report browsing; same-session generation and review of the Evidence DAG, Research Checkpoint, and Research Dossier still need to be confirmed in an actual run. - Data sources, Git commit, file hashes, and environment baseline - A cross-scale perturbation review table that preserves controls and missing states - A set of versioned figures generated from verified derived tables - A quality audit report, run manifest, and artifact inventory - An Evidence DAG linking claims, data, scripts, figures, and limitations - A human-reviewed Research Checkpoint and Research Dossier Verified data snapshot The following is the static baseline of the public demo copy cross-scale-data-demo@0696755 . A real run must recompute these values instead of hard-coding the numbers into scripts. Item Snapshot Runtime check --- ---: --- Total rows in the review table 35 Recomputed from the final TSV Unique target genes 15 Deduplicated after excluding non-targeting controls Perturbation guides / non-targeting controls 27 / 8 Check perturbation type explicitly L1 target and L2 pathway annotation 27/35 Output unmatched identifiers L3 transcriptional response 27/35 measured Separate unmeasured from no significant response L4 protein response 35/35 measured State that the ADT panel has only 4 markers L5 fitness endpoint 27/35 The 8 missing entries must not be zero-filled Quality checks 42 pass, 1 warning The warning points to the L5 missing rate Delivered artifacts 22 Count data, results, figures, scripts, reports, and manifests by category Workspace and artifact contract text cross-scale-data-demo/ ├── data/final/case45_cross_scale_integrated_dataset.tsv ├── data/processed/case45_l0_l5/case45_p0_20260708T1015Z/ └── run-output/ ├── scripts/ │ ├── stage01_source_inventory.py │ ├── stage02_reconstruct_dataset.py │ ├── stage03_quality_audit.py │ ├── stage04_context_expansion.py │ ├── stage05_generate_figures.py │ └── stage06_write_report.py ├── datasets/ ├── results/ ├── figures/ └── reports/case45_local_demo_report.md Every Stage should record its inputs, outputs, return code, and stop conditions. If the quality audit fails, do not continue to conclusion figures; figures must come from verified derived tables; and the final report must not hide warnings or unverified items. Figure 1: SciForge keeps the case workspace and task on the left, while the Files panel on the right expands the run-output/figures artifact tree. Permissions and baseline before you start This case creates scripts, tables, figures, and research records, so it requires "Can modify working directory"; the read-only sandbox from Getting started does not apply. Before you start, you must: 1. Use a case copy that can be published and redistributed. 2. Check git status --short and record the baseline commit. 3. Inventory the input files and record hashes, sources, and license boundaries. 4. Review the agent plan, output paths, and dependency requirements. 5. Do not install dependencies or access unlisted external services without confirmation. Full task prompt text Please complete one reviewable ECCITE-seq cross-scale perturbation analysis in the current workspace. Research question: compare the designated target genes against non-targeting controls and inspect the evidence relationships among target annotation, pathways, transcriptional response, protein response, and cell fitness. Execution requirements: 1. Check Git status first, inventory the data, scripts, and existing artifacts, and do not overwrite the original files. 2. Present the plan, output paths, and data quality checks before you start writing. 3. Preserve non-targeting controls and missing data; do not automatically fill missing values with zeros. 4. Produce a traceable perturbation review table that lists the source and transformation for each row. 5. Generate cross-layer coverage figures and key response figures from the review table, and save the figure versions. 6. Link claims, data, methods, figures, and limitations into the Evidence DAG. 7. Generate a Research Checkpoint and a Research Dossier, and list the causal conclusions that are not yet supported. Unless I explicitly allow it, do not install dependencies, do not access unlisted external services, and do not modify the raw data. Mark any data or conclusion you cannot verify as "unverified". Phase 1: Freeze sources and inspect the data The agent first inventories the data, scripts, and existing artifacts, then checks perturbation labels, controls, cell backgrounds, measured modalities, and missing values. The completion signal here is not a one-line "checks passed," but an inventory, a hash manifest, and a quality audit report you can open. Check specifically: - Non-targeting controls are not lost in a join or filter - missing is not conflated with the numeric value 0 - "Not measured" and "measured with no significant response" are expressed separately - Every external annotation records the provider, query conditions, and access date Figure 2: Viewing L0–L5 coverage and measurement status in SciForge; the workspace and task context remain in frame. Phase 2: Assemble the perturbation review table Connect perturbations, target annotation, pathways, and multimodal responses into one row-by-row traceable table. Recompute the row count, unique target gene count, control count, and per-layer coverage, and output the list of unmatched identifiers. If you only have a ready-made derived table without the complete raw counts, you must downgrade the task to "a traceable review of the existing derived results," and you must not claim that the full differential expression analysis was redone. Phase 3: Generate and inspect versioned figures All figures are generated from derived tables that passed the audit, and each records its input hash, script, parameters, and figure version. The same inputs and recipe should rebuild the same result. Figure 3: The file preview shows both the figure and the actual artifact path, so you can trace a result back to its input. When reading L3 and L4, do not give priority to the layer that "matches expectations better." A direction mismatch may come from time scale, measurement noise, or the coverage limits of the 4-marker ADT panel, and it should be preserved as a cross-layer separation result. Figure 4: Causal readiness, L3/L4 overlap, and the L5 effect distribution are inspected together in SciForge; this figure cannot support a causal claim on its own. Phase 4: Review the evidence and lock down delivery Connect each key claim to the original records, derived table, method script, and figure. Counter-evidence, missingness, and limitations should also become evidence nodes rather than being deleted from the final narrative. After the review passes: 1. Open Changes to verify the write scope. 2. Save an Artifact Version for the figures and key files. 3. Create a Research Checkpoint. 4. Record the research question, inputs, methods, results, limitations, and rerun procedure in the Research Dossier. Figure 5: The first screen of the final report shows stage status, the data baseline, the quality audit, and the artifact count. Conclusion writing template text Supported claims: - Which perturbation affected which layer of measurement, in which cell background? - Which original records, derived tables, methods, and figures directly support it? Candidate explanations: - Which pathway or mechanism could explain the result? - What assumptions does it depend on, and what validation is still missing? Claims that cannot be supported: - Why is the current data insufficient to support causal, generalized, or clinical conclusions? - What data, experiments, or independent reproduction is needed next? Failure paths and recovery Problem Wrong approach Correct handling --- --- --- L5 missing Fill with 0 and include in the average Keep the missing flag and report total N and evaluable N separately L3/L4 direction mismatch Keep only the layer that matches expectations better Keep the separated result and check the time scale and marker coverage Audit raises an error Keep plotting and write the Dossier Stop at the quality stage and rerun from the affected Stage after fixing External annotation unavailable Silently switch provider Use a frozen snapshot or stop, and flag freshness Raw counts incomplete Claim the full analysis was redone Downgrade to a traceable review of the existing derived table Completion criteria Use the following to accept your own run; they do not mean this page has already completed all continuous verification. - Baseline commit, input hashes, and environment records are available - The 35-row review table, 15 target genes, and 8 controls can be recomputed - Missing states and warnings are not hidden - Figures trace back to verified derived tables and generation scripts - Key claims have an evidence, counter-evidence, or unresolved status - Checkpoint, Dossier, and Git changes are reviewed together Related feature: Evidence & Reproducibility.

en.title: Anchored Comments
en.description: Select a piece of text, leave a comment, and come back to discuss and check it in place.
en.body: Anchored Comments Select a piece of text in a research record to leave a question, a suggested change, or review feedback on it. The comment keeps the selected text and the research-record entry it belongs to, so you can check back later. Add a comment These steps cover 0.2.3 . Enable a compatible plugin and make sure you have permission to save comments in this workspace. See Extension Center for installation. 1. Open the workspace and select the session containing the text. 2. Open Research record , and drag to select text within a single entry. 3. Click Add comment , and check the selected text shown in the panel and the research-record entry it belongs to. 4. Write your feedback and click Save . Discuss selection opens a chat draft that carries the selected text. To save it as a comment, use Add comment . If the panel already holds unsaved content, a new selection asks whether to keep or replace the draft. For example, select “Missing values were set to zero”, choose Add comment , and write “Check whether missing means not measured”. Save it and look up the comment in the session. The result should contain the quotation and your note. View, edit, and delete You can ask the Agent to list, view, or update the comments that already exist in the current workspace. The panel is mainly for creating new comments; to change an existing one, say in the session which comment to update and what to change. Deleting a comment requires confirmation. Comments are stored in the workspace and do not change the commented source file. After you switch projects, select the content you want to comment on again. Screenshots and feedback To include the current app view, take a screenshot separately in a client that supports it and has screenshot permission. Move account details, tokens, and other sensitive content out of view before capturing. Submitting feedback to an external service also needs separate confirmation. If no feedback service is configured, comments can only be saved and discussed locally. Tips - After the original text changes, re-check the quotation and its position. - Comments belong to the current workspace. Before sharing a project, check the comments and screenshots for content you do not want to share. - If Add comment is missing, check that the plugin is enabled, then select text within a single Research record entry in the current session. Related: Agent workflows, Plugin license terms.

en.title: Artifact Versions
en.description: Save independent versions of a single artifact such as a figure or data file, and compare or restore them at any time.
en.body: Artifact Versions Artifact Versions helps you keep different versions of the same figure, the same dataset, or any other file. Every save leaves an independent version, so you can view, compare, and restore it. After you change a workspace file, you need to save the artifact version again for this result to stay in the history. You can review the research process through Research Checkpoints, and check how a conclusion relates to its sources in Evidence DAG. Opening it - Entry: the Artifacts area of the workbench research summary lists recent artifacts; after selecting an entry, view its versions in the Research panel on the right. - Target: a single artifact in the current workspace, such as a figure, data, log, or code file. - Prerequisite: the session is bound to a workspace, and the Agent or the plugin that produced the artifact has already saved an artifact version. Save and check versions 1. Produce a figure or data in a task, and confirm the actual file is in the current workspace. 2. Have the Agent save an independent version of this artifact, and associate the inputs and related files used to produce it. 3. Find the artifact in the Artifacts list, open it, and check the currently selected version, the content digest, and the related files. 4. After changing the artifact, save again. In the Versions area of the research dossier, choose the two versions to compare, and check the differences in content and generation information. 5. When you need an older result, choose the historical version and restore it as a new version. Restoring keeps the existing history; afterwards, check the new version and the actual file state. Export and import Before delivery, explicitly choose the artifact versions to export in the research dossier, then export a Bundle. Exporting writes files, and the interface asks for confirmation first. Check that all the versions and related files the bundle needs are present, and that they are all allowed to be accessed and exported; if any required version is not visible or not allowed to be exported, the whole export fails. Validate the Bundle before importing it in the target workspace. Importing adds version records; a package with missing dependencies, inconsistent history, or damaged content is rejected. Before sharing, also check the bundle for data that should not be sent out. Tips - Only artifacts that have been saved appear in the version list. Scientific Figures keeps its own figure history and does not register it here automatically; when you need a link, save an artifact version separately. - Some versions reference workspace files. After a file is moved, changed, or deleted, viewing it may report a changed or missing source; check the actual file first. - Viewing, comparing, restoring, and importing are all limited by version access permissions. An entry in the history list may also be impossible to open or export. - A version record does not replace scientific review of the result; before delivery, still check the inputs, the methods, and the conclusions. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Dossier: view, compare, restore, and export selected versions. - Evidence DAG: use versions as the evidence and sources for claims. - Git Checkpoints: save the Git state of the whole workspace. - Workspaces and sessions: how a workspace limits the scope of artifacts.

en.title: Automation and scheduled tasks
en.description: Use scheduled tasks to repeat a single Agent instruction, or use Create Loop to organize multi-step flows.
en.body: Automation and scheduled tasks First verify in an ordinary session that the task completes correctly, then turn it into an automation. Define the output path and the operations that need confirmation up front, so that scheduled repeats do not overwrite files or submit twice. Automation has two entry points: Scheduled tasks is a built-in scheduling capability of the app, not a domain extension; Create Loop is a built-in flow tool for multi-node orchestration. Choose which one Need Entry point --- --- Run a single AI instruction daily, once, at an interval, or manually Scheduled tasks (this page) Connect AI tasks, conditions, HTTP requests, approvals, and subflows Create Loop Create a scheduled task Open Scheduled tasks from the left, click New task , and configure the name, instruction, model, reasoning effort, run time, and workspace in order. Figure 1: A scheduled task puts the task content, model, schedule, and runtime environment in a single configuration table. An instruction suitable for validation: Check the current workspace for newly appeared experiment logs and produce a summary of no more than three items. Do not modify the original logs; save the output to the prearranged reports directory. Scheduled tasks require SciForge to keep running and the computer to be awake at the trigger time. "Keep awake" only prevents suspension while a task is running; it cannot wake a computer that is already asleep. Create a Loop When you need multiple steps, open Create Loop from the right toolbar or More tools . For full instructions, see Create Loop (multi-step flows); the shortest path is: 1. Create a Loop and add AI task, condition, HTTP request, or manual approval nodes. 2. Define the input, output, and failure handling for each node. 3. Test a single node first, then run the whole flow manually. 4. Enable schedule triggers, Webhooks, or Agent hooks only after validation. Restarting the app loses a run that was paused at a manual approval node. For important flows, save each step's input, output, and result; before rerunning, check whether a file, request, or submission has already completed, to avoid writing or submitting twice. Automation acceptance - Workspace and output paths are explicit - Runtime, model, and Skill are fixed - The shortest task has already succeeded in an ordinary session - Individual nodes and the whole flow have each passed testing - External requests, writes, and credential use have approval boundaries - Recent results, errors, and recovery methods can be found When automation fails, do not start by increasing the retry count; first open the session and node results for the most recent run and determine whether the error will repeatedly produce external effects.

en.title: Biology Room
en.description: Pin sequences, structures, genome tracks, and annotations into a traceable workspace room.
en.body: Biology Room Biology Room ships with SciForge and needs no separate plugin. It organizes the sequences, structures, genome tracks, and annotations from biological samples or experimental material into one traceable room, for viewing, annotating, and handoff. In a session, have the Agent create or open a room, then view the files in it through file preview. A room stores asset references, selections, view state, and history, and has no separate panel today. Opening it - Entry point: an Agent invokes a Biology Room capability in a session to create or open a room; files inside the room are viewed through file preview. - Applies to: biological files and room manifests in the current workspace; paths must be workspace-relative. - Prerequisite: the workspace is writable; asset extensions are supported; when an index is referenced, the index lives in the same workspace as the source file. What it can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Create a room Give a title and optionally attach a first batch of assets Initial room manifest and revision 1 Open or create from a file Pass in one workspace file; reuse an existing room that already contains that file A new room, or the manifest of an existing room Add and manage assets Add or remove assets, or switch the current asset, against the current revision A new revision; asset fingerprint, format, modality, and readiness status Record selections and annotations Save sequence, structure, or genome selections and view state, and bind annotation anchors Structured selections, view state, and annotations stored by anchor Refresh and roll back Refresh asset fingerprints; view history and restore a revision Updated revision, orphaned annotation markers, and history events Typical workflow 1. List existing rooms first and check whether a room already contains the target file, to avoid creating duplicates. 2. Open or create a room from the file; verify the returned path, format, SHA-256, and index fingerprint. 3. Commit a set of changes against the current revision, using dry-run mode first to see whether there are changes and warnings. 4. After applying the changes, read the room again and verify the revision, asset readiness, and annotation anchors. 5. Refresh the room after source files change; to roll back, view history first, then restore the older revision to produce a new revision number. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Read: FASTA/GenBank, PDB/mmCIF, and GFF3/BED/VCF files in the workspace, optionally with .fai , .gzi , .tbi , and .csi indexes; up to 4 indexes per asset. - Write: room manifests, revision snapshots, and event logs, stored in the room directory under .sciforge/biology/rooms/ in the workspace; source files are referenced read-only. - Approval or external effects: room writes touch workspace metadata only and do not trigger approval; put human confirmation before dry-run review, cascading asset removal, and restoring an old revision. - What it will not do: modify or delete source files, perform alignment, variant calling, or structural computation, or provide real-time multi-user collaboration; removing an asset removes only the room reference. Known limitations - Narrower support than Life Science Preview: no FASTQ, GTF, omics matrices, imaging, or spectra; gzip covers only FASTA, GFF, BED, and VCF. - A room holds at most 128 assets, 2,000 annotations, and 100 MiB of assets in total; a single unindexed asset is capped at 25 MiB. - Rooms have no standalone interface; creation, changes, and restoration all happen through the Agent in a session. - After a refresh, missing or unreadable assets are marked explicitly, and annotations that lost their anchor are marked orphaned and need human confirmation before you handle them. - Applying changes validates the revision number and rejects stale ones; history is stored by revision and may be truncated. - The collaboration boundary is sharing one room manifest and version history, not cloud-based real-time multi-user collaboration. Related pages - Life Science Preview: dedicated views for sequences, structures, and genome files in a room. - Acquiring and organizing data: download data and record its source, date, version, license, and verification results. - Workspaces and sessions: workspace location, file paths, and recovery boundaries. - Evidence & Reproducibility: fold room changes into the larger research record chain. Current version: built-in Biology Workbench 1.1.3. For what selection saving covers in the molecular preview, see Life Science Preview.

en.title: Browser Preview
en.description: Open web pages inside the app so the Agent can browse and act on pages that are visible and subject to approval.
en.body: Browser Preview Open a web page in the right panel of the SciForge desktop app. Browse and sign in yourself, or use the session to tell the assistant what to read or do on the page. Open a page 1. Click Browser in the far-right toolbar. Open More tools if it is out of view, or open Native browser in the right panel. If a development page in a regular browser says native preview is unavailable, open the SciForge desktop app. 2. Enter an HTTP(S) address and press Enter. The address bar shows the current URL. Use the panel controls to go back or forward, reload, or go full screen. 3. Sign in within the panel if the site requires it. Sessions in the same workspace share its browser sign-in. Use the site's account menu to see which account is active. Sign in separately for accounts used in an external browser. Each native browser instance opens one page. Use the address bar to identify the active page when you switch panels. Read a page Send a link in the session and specify what to find. For example, ask for a dataset's release date. The assistant first tries a read-only HTTP(S) request from your device. If the content needs sign-in or script rendering, open it in the Browser panel and direct the session to the current page. Use the title, URL, or quotations in the reply to find the source. <details <summary What the browser can read</summary The initial read-only URL request requires no extra confirmation. Browser tools can read text, titles, URLs, and controls, and can take screenshots. The read excludes password, payment, CAPTCHA, and marked sensitive fields. For a chart rendered on a canvas, a cross-origin iframe, or a closed shadow root, use a screenshot or inspect the page yourself. Instructions displayed on a site are page content. Actions follow the task you set in the session. </details Take an action on a site 1. Open the target page. Tell the assistant which site to use and what you want to do. Approve the prompt when the assistant navigates, goes back or forward, or reloads. The address bar then shows the current URL. 2. Fill in a draft. Name the fields to fill and where to stop. For example, fill in the title and stop at the submit button. You can also ask the assistant to pause before sending, paying, deleting, or uploading something you want to review. 3. Submit and look for a receipt. State which data the assistant may send. After submission, look in the panel for the site’s receipt, success message, or destination page. Check the result before retrying. 4. Download a file. Specify the download link in the session. The reply shows the file name and path after the download. With a workspace open, look in Files for the session folder under .sciforge-downloads . Without a workspace, open the returned path under the app’s browser-downloads directory. <details <summary Page controls, pop-ups, and script debugging</summary On an authorized page, the browser can click, type, press keys, or drag. Enter can submit a form, and dropping a file can start an upload. The browser blocks permission requests, pop-ups, and downloads initiated by the page itself. To download a blocked file, use an explicit download link. Use separate developer tools to debug page scripts. </details Related pages - Workbench tools - Permissions and security - Computer Use - Remote resources and collaboration Component version: @sciforge/domain-browser-preview v1.0.8.

en.title: Change Inspector
en.description: Check which file changes the current task recorded, and verify the actual content item by item.
en.body: Change Inspector Change Inspector helps you check which files the current task changed and what changed in each one. After you install and enable the plugin, you can ask the Agent directly to list the changes, then verify them item by item. How to use it These steps cover 0.1.3 . Enable a compatible plugin, then try it in the same session that recorded a file edit. See Extension Center for installation. 1. In a demo workspace, ask the Agent to make one edit, such as adding a review note to notes.md . 2. In the same session, ask: Check which files this task changed, and explain each change. If the content is too long, show it in batches and tell me what is not yet shown. 3. The change list should include notes.md , and its diff should show the added line. Open the next batch if the list continues. If it is empty, return to the session that made the edit, then open the file or check Git status. Tips - The list shows edits recorded in the current session. Use the actual files or Git status to look for manual edits or changes from another tool or session. - When there are many files or changes, what is shown may be incomplete. First confirm what has not yet been shown, then keep checking in batches; do not rebuild a whole file from partial diffs alone. - If more edits happen during the review, refresh the file change list and re-check the affected files. - After you disable the plugin or revoke its permissions, you must enable it again or re-authorize it to continue checking. After checking Change Inspector only reads records; it does not modify files, roll back, save checkpoints, or make network requests. When you find a problem, have the Agent change the file in question and then check again. To restore the workspace state, see Git Checkpoints. Related: Evidence & Reproducibility, Permissions & security, Plugin license terms.

en.title: Collaboration guide
en.description: Starting from requirements and task assignment, complete member task acceptance, human review, deliverable acceptance, and project close-out.
en.body: Collaboration guide The project owner uses Requirements to define the deliverables and the Board to assign and review tasks. The assigned member adds the required files and submits or revises the delivery. The next member works from the upstream version the owner accepted. Open a collaboration project 1. Expand the left sidebar and use the account area at the bottom to sign in and connect your device. Each member uses their own account. 2. Open a project, My work , or Inbox from the collaboration section. The project name appears at the top, and its tasks appear on the Board . 3. Before accepting a task, send a short message in a regular session. Once your Runtime and model return a reply, open the assignment. Project tab Use it to --- --- Board Find tasks and see their assignment, delivery, and review status Members Invite or manage people as allowed by your role Requirements Define the goal, inputs, modules, and acceptance criteria Shared files Open shared material, sealed deliveries, and project results Project details See the project details and available management actions The collaboration service receives requirements, project discussions, result notes, and submitted files. The local workspace remains on your device. Store credentials in the corresponding service settings. 1. The owner prepares and confirms requirements 1. In the collaboration sidebar, click + and enter a project name. 2. Open Requirements . Under Goals and deliverables and Inputs and boundaries , list the data the member can access, the file names to deliver, acceptance criteria, and the allowed actions. 3. Click Save requirements . Once drafted, Work modules and Acceptance criteria list each module's inputs, required file, prerequisites, and verification criteria; review them and click Confirm requirements . If generation fails, resolve the error shown on the page, then click Complete with AI (AI 补全) to retry. 4. Invite people from Members . Invitees open the request from Inbox or the project invitation and click Accept invitation . Their names then appear under Members . For example, assign B a report on per-sample counts, including the method and results. Make C's module depend on the owner accepting B's report. Requirements show which module must be accepted before the next can start. 2. Check assignments and blocking reasons As the owner, open the task from the Board . If the assignee is available and the upstream delivery is accepted, choose the member and click Dispatch task . The card moves to Ready and shows the assigned member. If dispatch fails, address the reason shown in the task and click Dispatch again . Before the member accepts an assignment, you can Reassign or Withdraw assignment . What the task shows What to do --- --- Waiting for an upstream delivery to be accepted Open the upstream task and review the latest delivery. After accepting it, return to the downstream task. Unassigned, or dispatch failed because there is no eligible member Choose an assignee or complete the requested assignment action. The card then shows the assigned member under Ready . 3. Members decide whether to accept Open the request from Inbox , My work , the Board task card, or the task details. Read the goal, required files, dependencies, and expiry before responding. Action Result --- --- Accept task The task is yours. When the Runtime is ready, the task session shows execution progress. Follow the message if the Runtime needs attention. Dismiss The request is removed from the relevant lists for your account. Reject The owner can arrange a new assignment. Dismiss the board reminder if you just want to close it. If the assignment has expired, ask the owner for a new one. 4. Handle agent questions and action confirmations - Answer a question. The requested member opens the task details, supplies the missing data or decision, and returns to the task session to follow progress. - Decide on an action. Open the request in the task details. Check what it will change or send, where it will act, and which version it covers. Check when it expires. Say why you’re approving or rejecting it, then click Approve action or Reject action . If the request has expired, wait for a new one. After approval, return to the task session to see the result. Use the action buttons for authorization. Discussions can provide context. 5. Members review the draft and submit 1. Open the delivery draft in the task details and preview the required files. If Submit is unavailable, the submission area names the missing file. Where Choose required file is available, pick a task output or upload a file, then click 用作必交文件 (Use as required file). It appears in the required files list, where you can click Preview to inspect it. 2. In Result summary , describe what you did, the checks you ran, and the scope of the result. For another revision in the task session, click Work with AI , then return to the draft. 3. To include a separate note, click Add materials → Task files or Upload from this device . Each submission allows up to 20 files (including the required file) and 200 MiB in total, with up to 100 MiB per attachment. Required files follow the task's format and size requirements. 4. Click Submit . In the dialog, review the version number, summary, and files. Click Submit again to send that version. After signing and upload, the version appears in the delivery section and the task moves to Awaiting review on the Board. The task details show Awaiting confirmation . If the system prompts for secure storage access, the member responds. The draft groups result notes, required files, and additional materials. The submission shows device verification, signing, and upload progress. 6. The owner reviews and hands off downstream 1. Review the latest submission. Open the task from Board → Awaiting review . Read Result summary in the submission at the top of the delivery section. Click Preview beside each file and compare it with the acceptance criteria. 2. Request specific changes. Click Request revision , describe which part needs work, and click Send revision request . The member updates the files and submits a new version. Open the new submission at the top of the delivery section. Use Version history to see the previous submission. 3. Accept the version that meets the criteria. Click Adopt delivery (采纳交付) . The task moves to Completed , and the delivery section shows Adopted and the version number. 4. Hand off the accepted version. After adopting the upstream delivery, the owner dispatches the downstream task. The next member clicks Accept task and goes to their task session. The accepted files are in the task’s working directory in the Files panel on the right. The request identifies what the member needs to change. Use the latest submission for review and the accepted one for downstream work. 7. View shared files and close out Under Shared files , find and preview files by source and version. To submit your own files, attach them from the task’s delivery draft with Add materials . Once every module is accepted, click Complete project . Fill in Completion summary and click Confirm completion . After signing, the project status changes to Completed . Both deliveries are accepted, and the project shows Completed. Board status at a glance Column Who acts next --- --- Backlog The owner resolves dependencies or selects an assignee. Ready The assigned member responds to the dispatch. In progress The member follows execution, answers questions, or reviews the draft. Awaiting review The delivery is submitted and awaiting the owner. Completed The delivery is accepted. The owner can close the project when every task is complete. For a network, submission, or signing error, keep the draft and restore account and device access. Then open the delivery section in the task details. If this version is present, it can go to review. If only the draft remains, return to the task details and submit it again. Continue with the Pasilla case study, Identity and sign-in, or Runtime and models.

en.title: Computer Use
en.description: Enable Computer Use so Codex or Claude Code can operate browser and in-app embedded pages within the scope you authorize.
en.body: Computer Use Computer Use lets the Agent observe a page and click, type, press keys, or scroll step by step, which suits tasks that must be done through an interface. It currently supports Codex and Claude Code only , and its scope is browser pages and the embedded pages of Electron apps, such as Browser Preview; it cannot be used to operate arbitrary desktop applications. Enable and check 1. Open Settings → AI assistant → Computer use , turn on the main switch, and choose Codex or Claude Code for this use. 2. Check the run status on the settings page; if it is unavailable, handle the page's prompt first. 3. In macOS System Settings, grant the Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions, then return to the app and confirm the status. 4. Open the target page, and in the session state the task, the allowed actions, the stopping conditions, and the forbidden actions. Figure 1: Enable Computer Use on the settings page, and check its run status and system permissions. Run a task 1. First have the Agent observe the current page, and check the page identity and the target content. 2. Carry out actions step by step. Every call that changes state needs your confirmation; check the specific action before allowing it, because a confirmation does not authorize later actions of the same kind. 3. Before signing in, authorizing, sending, uploading, buying, paying, deleting, or submitting a formal result, confirm the target of the action and its consequences. 4. When done, stop the task or release the session, and go back to the page to check the actual result. What actions affect, and tips - Observation reads the page content, interactive elements, and screenshots; read-only queries need no confirmation. - Clicking, typing, key presses, and scrolling act directly on the target page and may submit something or change the page state. - Pages and screenshots may contain accounts, patient information, or unpublished data; check and redact before sharing or exporting. Do not have the Agent fill in passwords, verification codes, or payment information. - When the run status is unavailable or system permissions are insufficient, fix the problem before continuing the task. - When the session ends, the current operating connection is released. Computer Use is not suited to unattended, long-running automation. Related pages - Permissions & security: system permissions and confirmation of key actions. - Skills, MCP, and Extensions: tool connections and extension management. - Browser Preview: the main page entry that can currently be operated. - Workbench tools: how the tools divide the work, and usage principles. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-computer-use v1.0.1.

en.title: Content Space
en.description: View the connected note service and choose an open notebook in SiYuan.
en.body: Content Space Content Space is for viewing the connected note service and choosing a notebook. It currently supports SiYuan Notes, and lists only notebooks that are open and not closed in SiYuan. The note content stays in the original SiYuan service. Open it and choose a notebook 1. First connect your own SiYuan service as described on the SiYuan Notes page. 2. Open Content Space in the right panel; Shared files on the full Collaboration page also provides this entry. 3. Choose the connected SiYuan service, then choose a notebook from the list. If you cannot find the one you want, first confirm in SiYuan that the notebook is open. 4. To read, edit, or search documents, open the SiYuan Notes page, or have the Agent use SiYuan's search, read, and write tools. Tips - Content Space currently offers notebook selection only; you cannot browse or edit SiYuan documents, or upload or download files, here. - The Shared files entry also has no direct upload button for now. Choosing a notebook does not send local files into SiYuan. - When the connection is no longer valid, first check the SiYuan service address and connection status, then reconnect. - Document edits and Agent writes affect the connected SiYuan service; before acting, confirm the target notebook and document. Related pages - SiYuan Notes: connect the service, edit and search, and archive tasks. - Collaboration: how Shared files relates to task delivery files. - Permissions & security: external writes and confirmation rules. - Feature status and limitations: the current status of each capability. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-content-space v5.0.4.

en.title: Create Loop (multi-step workflows)
en.description: Chain AI, conditions, HTTP, and human approvals in multi-node workflows.
en.body: Create Loop (multi-step workflows) Try a loop that turns a short note into three lines, then pauses for you to approve the result. Once that works, you can add a file write or an external request after the approval. How to open it Click Create Loop in the far-right toolbar. Look under More Tools if the icon is out of view. Name the loop and choose its working directory in the canvas settings. AI, image, and code nodes use this directory. The definition and run records are stored on your device. Typical workflow This example sends the three lines to an Output node after approval. Both a trial run and Test node execute the configured nodes. AI nodes send requests to the model provider. HTTP nodes send requests to the configured address. These requests may incur fees. Start with short text and leave out anything that writes to an external system. 1. Set up the Runtime. Configure an available Runtime in Settings → AI Assistants . Once it can reply in a regular session, return to the canvas. 2. Add and connect the nodes. Add Manual trigger , AI agent task , Human Approval , and Output from the left side. Connect the first three nodes in order. Connect the Approved output to Output , and leave Rejected unconnected. 3. Give the AI node one sample. Select AI agent task , pick a model, and enter a short note in Prompt . Example input: “Monday: entered the sample table. Tuesday: standardized the units. Wednesday: reviewed missing values. Summarize each day in one line.” You can use Test node on the AI node to see whether it returns three lines. Testing saves the loop first. 4. Set up human approval. Select Human Approval and enter a title, instructions, and timeout. In this example, approve when all three days are represented and the lines match the source. 5. Run the loop and decide. Click Run once and confirm. When the run pauses, open the request with the approval title and Approve and Reject buttons on the card or in the run drawer. Read the upstream result. If it meets the criteria, click Approve . The pause ends, Output receives the three lines, and the run shows Success when it finishes. Click Reject if something is missing. The Output node is skipped. 6. Open the result. In Run log , open Output to see the three lines. Find the run in Run history and use Audit report if you need the inputs, outputs, or timings. Run one representative sample end to end before processing a batch. The Approved port leads to Output. The right panel shows the approval instructions for this example. What you can do Task Where to configure it --- --- Generate content or run an agent task Add LLM generation or AI agent task , then enter the inputs and the result you need. Branch based on the data Add Condition , a multi-way branch, merge, filter, or loop. Select the upstream node that supplies each input. Call an external service Add HTTP request and set the destination and permissions. Put Human Approval before the request if someone needs to approve it. Reuse an existing flow Add a subworkflow and select the loop and its inputs. Start automatically After a successful trial run, turn on Enabled . Set up a schedule or webhook, enable AI Callable , or configure an Agent hook. Scheduled and local webhook triggers require the app to stay running. Where things are saved, and what actions affect - Before running, set the working directory, timeouts, output paths, and how to handle failures. Save results you need later to the workspace. - Follow the app's confirmation when stopping the run or deciding an approval. Nodes that use a Secret need that credential to rerun. The run history hides the original value. - Restarting the app ends a run paused for approval. Open Run history to see which nodes completed. If any already wrote files or submitted a request, start a new loop with the saved output and only the remaining steps. To repeat this text-only example, run it again from Manual trigger . - If randomness is unfixed, differences between runs are marked inconclusive. Fix randomness before comparing runs for reproducibility. Related pages - Automation and scheduled tasks - Evidence and reproducibility - Agent workflows - Permissions and security Component version: @sciforge/domain-create-loop v1.1.4.

en.title: Acquiring and organizing data
en.description: Obtain data with the provider's client or your own scripts, and keep records of source, version, license, and verification.
en.body: Acquiring and organizing data Use a client the data provider supports, or run a download script in an environment you have configured. First confirm access rights, terms of use, and the storage space you need; manage credentials as described in Permissions & security. 1. Confirm the data source URL, the data version, and the license, and record the access or download date. 2. Download with the provider's client or a script, and keep the commands, download parameters, and results actually used. 3. Check the file size and SHA-256; when the provider publishes checksums, compare against them one by one and record the verification result. 4. When organizing files, keep the original data. Save cleaning, filtering, or format conversions as separate results, and record how inputs, processing scripts, and outputs correspond. Supported downloaded files can be viewed in Life Science Preview, and Biology Room can organize the sequence, structure, and genome assets it supports. Previewing and organizing assets do not replace downloading, integrity checks, or analysis. Data acquisition, cleaning, and scientific conclusions each need real execution and source records; see Evidence & reproducibility.

en.title: Evidence & Reproducibility
en.description: Use artifact versions, checkpoints, Evidence DAG, and Research Dossier to pin down the research process and results.
en.body: Evidence & Reproducibility SciForge keeps a research task's inputs, process, and results through artifact versions, run records, and source links, so you can recheck them and continue the research. Choose a recording method as you need. Artifact versions, checkpoints, the evidence graph, and the research dossier use built-in entry points in the app; Change Inspector needs a plugin installed and enabled. For version requirements, see Version & Compatibility. Recording feature Purpose and how it is provided --- --- Artifact Versions Save independent versions of a single artifact; compare and restore earlier results Git Checkpoints Automatically save the Git workspace state at the start and end of a task Research Checkpoints Automatically save the research summary, sources, and file references of completed turns Change Inspector Use a plugin to check the file changes already recorded in the current session Evidence DAG Save and check the conclusions and evidence relationships in the current session Project DAG Manually combine the evidence graphs each session has saved, to check project progress Research Dossier Read a selected research record, check versions and limitations, and prepare delivery Choose the right record object Object Problem it solves Typical content --- --- --- Session How did the task progress? Messages, tool calls, commands, approvals, and the final response Artifact Version How did a figure or file evolve? Artifact path, version, inputs, and generation details Git Checkpoint What stage are the workspace files at? Git status and stage-level code snapshots Research Checkpoint How do I continue a research stage? Research context, key artifacts, and resume location Evidence DAG What supports or refutes a claim? Claims, sources, methods, artifacts, limitations, and relationships Research Dossier How does someone else read the final deliverable? Research question, inputs, methods, results, credibility, and limitations Build a checkable chain Recommended order: 1. At the start of the task, record the workspace, input versions, and objective; a Git workspace automatically saves a checkpoint from before the task started. 2. After the analysis, save the actual sources, commands, parameters, result files, and figures, and save independent versions of the artifacts you want to keep. 3. Wait for this round's research record to be saved, then open the research dossier to check the summary, references, and selected versions. Confirm the summary record and the actual files separately. 4. In Evidence DAG, click Update , wait for the evidence graph to finish saving, then check item by item the relationship between conclusions and sources, counter-evidence, and missing information. 5. When you need a cross-session summary, first confirm each session's evidence graph is saved, then click Update now in Project DAG; after it finishes, review the current project graph. 6. In the research dossier, check the selected record and its limitations, and before delivery verify the related files, versions, and sharing permissions. Figure 1: The research dossier shows the research narrative, selected versions, a credibility summary, and the limitations that need attention together. Have the Agent leave a complete record You can add this to a task: After the analysis, organize the research question, input files, methods used, key parameters, results, and limitations into the research dossier. Every key conclusion should trace back to its source, derived table, or figure; mark anything you cannot confirm as unverified. Do not only ask it to "generate an Evidence DAG". First make clear which claims deserve review, which data can directly support them, and which explanations are still candidate hypotheses. Manual review checklist - Can every key number be traced back to the input files and the computation steps? - Do the figures come from verified derived tables, not intermediate files edited by hand? - Does the conclusion confuse correlation, prediction, and causation? - Are counter-evidence, warnings, and missing data still visible? - Are the code commit, environment, parameters, and random seed needed for a rerun complete? - Does each checkpoint correspond to a Git state you have already checked? Before you rely on it A standalone plugin must be installed and enabled first. For installation requirements, see the plugin list. For the evidence graph, use the built-in entry point in the app. The optional standalone Evidence DAG plugin cannot yet be used fully in the app; for the availability and licenses of optional plugins, see the plugin list. Scientific Figures saves its own code, inputs, environment, runs, and image history, and does not register them with Artifact Versions or Evidence DAG automatically. When you include a figure in a deliverable, link the actual inputs, runs, and outputs explicitly, and recheck them before forming a claim. Data boundary Evidence DAG and Research Dossier show meaningful content only when the current workspace and session already have the matching data. An empty panel does not mean the feature is broken; first have the task produce clear claims, sources, and artifact records. Case: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence graph.

en.title: Evidence DAG
en.description: See which sources, analysis steps, and result files support a session's conclusions, and what limitations remain.
en.body: Evidence DAG Evidence DAG helps you check what a conclusion rests on: in the graph, see the sources, computation steps, figures, and limitations that support or refute it. First finish the analysis and save the sources, results, and related files, then click Update to save the evidence graph; after the update finishes, separately check the relationships and gaps in the graph. To combine several sessions, use Project DAG. Opening it - Entry: in the Research panel, click View evidence graph . When the standalone evidence panel is open, switch from the default Research record to Evidence graph . - Target: the evidence graph already saved in the current session. - Prerequisite: the task has left sources, an analysis process, and result records, and the evidence-graph feature and the text-reasoning configuration are available. Save and check the evidence graph 1. Finish a round of analysis, and save the sources actually used, the computation records, the result files, and the matching artifact versions; make clear which are conclusions and which are still hypotheses. 2. Click Update , wait for queueing and execution to finish, and confirm the new evidence graph has been saved. Updating calls the configured text-reasoning service and saves evidence records, with no extra approval. 3. In the graph, select a conclusion and its related nodes, and check item by item whether the sources, runs, code, environment, and artifact versions support it. Even after a successful save, this review is still yours to do. 4. Check whether the conclusion can be traced to its sources, find missing records and known limitations, and handle the prompts about a missing source, an unverified version, or a missing approval. After adding real records, update again and check the result. 5. To combine several sessions, first confirm this session's evidence graph has been saved, then go to Project DAG and update the project graph manually. Further checks - Click Audit to check the structure of the saved evidence graph and see the gap hints. For now it only checks the graph's structure (L0); you still have to judge whether a conclusion has a scientific basis. - Select a Conclusion node and click Download rerun spec to download the configuration notes needed to rerun the analysis. Before rerunning, also confirm that the input files, software, parameters, environment, and related result files are available; downloading the spec does not run the analysis. - To check whether an analysis can be rerun under its original conditions, verify that the input files, software versions, parameters, environment, run records, logs, and result files are complete and verifiable. If the analysis involves randomness, reaching the L4 reproducibility level also requires recording the random seed. A random seed alone is not enough: the files and records listed above must also be complete and verifiable. Tips - If no claims, sources, or artifacts have been saved yet, the graph may be empty. Save the analysis records and actual files first, then update the evidence graph. - If an update fails, you can keep viewing the graph saved before, but make sure you know which result you are reviewing. Only a saved graph can be used for audit. - When a source or run record is missing, the graph shows a prompt. Go back to the actual source and run records to check; a chat summary alone cannot fill the gap. - Restricted evidence may not be previewable, and you should respect the source's access permissions. - Rebuilding is only for upgrades, corruption recovery, or reinterpretation, and needs a stated reason and justification; for everyday additions to the record, use Update. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Project DAG: combine the evidence graphs several sessions have saved into a project view. - Research Dossier: read research records and prepare delivery. - Artifact Versions: save the artifact versions that evidence references. - Virtual cell evidence atlas case: how evidence is organized in a complete task.

en.title: Skills, MCP, and Extensions
en.description: See where capabilities come from in the Extension Center, manage extensions and Skills, and check MCP and desktop-control permissions.
en.body: Skills, MCP, and Extensions Open Extensions for tools and panels. Use Skills to reuse a method, and MCP to connect a session to an external tool or data source. Open the Extension Center Expand the left sidebar and click Extensions . Opening an entry shows its publisher, version, source, status, permissions, and contributed tools or panels. Open extension pages from the left navigation and tool panels from the toolbar on the far right. For a file-preview extension, open a file of the supported type from Files . If an icon is out of view, open More tools . Use Customize toolbar to move supported tools. Dockable pages can sit on the left, right, bottom, or in the main area. Open Extensions from the left sidebar to see where an item comes from. Open an entry to see its version, source, and status. Check availability, install, and enable What you want to do Where to go and what you get --- --- Find out what a plugin does and see its compatibility status Open the SciForge public catalog and select the entry to see its supported tasks and public status. Install a DSH plugin in the desktop app Open Extensions → Market . Installable entries show Install . The Market supplies .sciforge-dsh-plugin packages. Use a bundled module Open its entry in Extensions to see whether it is enabled and where to open it. Install a signed extension from a local file Open Extensions → Install from file and select a supported .sciforge-plugin package. The app verifies its publisher, signature, and version compatibility. Install from the desktop Market. Open an installable entry to review its publisher, version, tool permissions, and requested Host operations, then click Install → Approve and install . Once the entry shows Enabled , open its entry point and run a quick check. Existing plugins can be enabled, disabled, uninstalled, or rolled back from their detail page. If the app requests a restart, restart before opening the entry point. In Extensions → Market , expand Not installable yet to see why an entry is unavailable. Follow the maintainer’s instructions for development builds. See Versions and compatibility for the build and Market index shown in the screenshot. Expand Not installable yet to see the reason for each entry. Plugin tutorials Try these examples with a compatible, enabled version of the DSH plugin. - Anchored Comments. In a workspace where you can save comments, open Research record and select “Missing values were filled with 0” within one entry. Click Add comment , write “Check whether a blank means the sample was not measured,” and click Save (保存批注) . To find the comment again, query it in the session. The result should contain both the quoted text and your note. See Anchored Comments. - Change Inspector. Use a session in a demo workspace to add a line to notes.md . In the same session, request the recorded changes. The list should include notes.md , and its diff should show the added line. Open the next batch if the list continues. See Change Inspector. - Scientific Figures. Use a writable local workspace, a configured DSH session, and Python with Matplotlib on a macOS system that passes the execution checks. Open Scientific Figures → New → Start from data , run the sample, and click Refresh to see the PNG in Figures . See Scientific Figures. Use a Skill Open Extensions → Skills to find a method. Before enabling it, review its project or global scope, trigger conditions, and the scripts, software, materials, or credentials it uses. If it installs dependencies, accesses the network, or writes files, check the requested scope in the approval prompt when it runs. Try a small sample first and compare the output file or reply against the Skill's criteria. See the Skills available to the current project or globally. Connect an MCP Server 1. Expand the left sidebar and open Settings → AI assistant to identify the Runtime used in the session. If it supports custom servers, follow its instructions to open its MCP settings. You can also use the MCP tools already available in the session. 2. In a Runtime that supports custom connections, open its MCP server settings and enter the startup command or server address. Before saving, review five items: the service's source, version, launch method or address, credential scope, and what data the tool reads, writes, or sends. Enter credentials in the configuration's credential input. 3. Return to the session and use the service for a read-only query, such as listing a resource you know exists. The result should include that resource's name or ID. Before sending, uploading, deleting, or writing anything, specify the target, data destination, and authorization. Afterward, open the target system to see the added or updated item. Use Computer Use With Codex or Claude Code, enable Computer Use in Settings and look at its status. On macOS, check Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions. Identify the browser page or embedded Electron page and what can be done there. Review any login, authorization, payment, send, or delete action when it comes up, then look for its result on the page. Settings show whether Computer Use is enabled and which system permissions it needs. When you cannot find a feature Open Extensions to see whether the entry shows Enabled , an error, or a restart prompt, and check your workspace permissions and Runtime support. If the tool panel is out of view, open More tools or Customize toolbar . If an enabled Skill or MCP tool does not appear in a session, start a new session. For a local installation failure, fix the package format, signature, publisher, or version shown in the error message and install again. Related pages: Workbench tools and Permissions and security.

en.title: Git Checkpoints
en.description: Automatically save Git checkpoints at the start and end of a task, and leave a rescue snapshot before restoring.
en.body: Git Checkpoints Git Checkpoints automatically saves the workspace's Git state at the start and end of a task turn, so you can check what this turn changed and, when needed, restore an earlier state. For the research summary, sources, and where to continue the research, see Research Checkpoints. Opening it - Entry: Git Checkpoints in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown); the right panel is titled Git Checkpoints as well. - Target: the local Git workspace bound to the current session. - Prerequisite: the workspace is a Git repository and Git features are available; a non-Git workspace produces no checkpoints. View and restore 1. Start a task in a Git workspace, and the system automatically saves a checkpoint from before the start; you do not need to save one by hand or keep the panel open. 2. After the task turn finishes or ends, open the panel or click the refresh icon, and check the records from before the start and after the end. 3. Select a checkpoint, read the file differences and the change summary, and confirm it matches the state you want to restore. 4. When you need to restore, click Restore and confirm. The system first saves a rescue checkpoint; if saving fails, the restore is aborted. 5. After restoring, check the actual workspace files and the Git status. To see the file changes the current task recorded, you can use Change Inspector. Confirm before restoring Restoring rewrites workspace files, so first confirm the target checkpoint, and check whether there are changes you still need to keep. The rescue checkpoint saves the state from before the restore, so you can get back the work that this restore overwrote. The panel offers a list, a diff preview, refresh, and restore, with no button to create a checkpoint by hand. The diff preview may show only part of the content; when a preview is incomplete, check the actual files and the Git diff further before restoring. What is saved A Git checkpoint saves the workspace's Git state, which suits reviewing code and file changes. The research question, sources, and next-step plan still need to be recorded through research checkpoints; versions of a single figure or data file can be saved separately as Artifact Versions. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Checkpoints: save research context and the resume location. - Artifact Versions: save versions of a single artifact. - Change Inspector: check which file changes a session recorded. - Workspaces and sessions: how the workspace, sessions, and Git state relate.

en.title: Identity & Access
en.description: Manage the local account, cloud sign-in, device connection, and usage summary from the bottom of the sidebar.
en.body: Identity & Access Expand the workbench's left sidebar and look at the bottom for the local account, cloud status, and usage summary . Click the account row to open the account panel; click the cloud row to open the same panel positioned at SciForge Cloud . Settings sits below it. A local account is an attribution marker To use local features, create or select a local account in the account panel and set its display name. Use the same panel to rename or sign out of that account. On a shared computer, use separate operating-system accounts to isolate workspaces, chats, settings, API keys, and tool data. The SciForge local account marks attribution. To join a collaboration project, sign in to the cloud and connect the device as described below. The delete button on an account row first shows a confirmation area. Once confirmed, it deletes that local account and its attribution data on this machine, and this cannot be undone. When you delete the current account, the system selects the earliest-created remaining account; after the last account is deleted, no account is selected. Delete account here is local identity management. It is not cloud account cancellation, project deletion, or workspace file cleanup. Signing out of a local account, signing out of the cloud, and disconnecting a device each do something different, so check the button name and its target before acting. Sign in to the cloud and connect a device 1. Create or choose a local account first. Until one is selected, "Browser sign-in" is unavailable. 2. Under SciForge Cloud , click Browser sign-in and complete authentication in the system browser. You do not need to paste a password or token into a session. 3. After returning, check the cloud identity. If no device is connected yet, click Connect this device . 4. Collaboration features that depend on cloud identity can continue only when the identity is valid and the device is active. The local account, the model provider sign-in, and the SciForge cloud sign-in are separate configurations. Cloud features depend on the current app configuration and service availability.
