Panel state or action Meaning and what to do --- --- Not signed in to the cloud Local features still work; cloud projects need sign-in This device is not connected Being signed in is not a device connection; connect the device from the interface Connecting this device Wait for the device registration result and avoid repeating the action This device is connected The device is active; a valid cloud identity and project permission are still required This device is disconnected / connection error Cloud permissions cannot be used as if connected normally; check the error and recover as prompted Sign in again Completes cloud authentication again; it does not automatically accept project invitations or tasks Sign out Clears the current cloud sign-in session; do not treat it as having revoked the device registration Disconnect this device Revokes this device's cloud access; local features are kept When a device is revoked, the identity changes, or device validity cannot be confirmed, cloud authentication rights are withdrawn. Do not use a cached display name to decide you are still authorized. If sign-in or connection fails, retry as the panel suggests and keep the original task and drafts. Reading the usage summary The bottom of the sidebar shows token and cost summaries for today and the last 7 days recorded on this machine; for the actual charges, check the model provider's bill. Loading, no data, and load failure each show their own message. No data does not mean no model requests were made. Credentials and recovery boundaries Cloud sign-in material and device keys are managed by the platform's secure storage. When secure storage is unavailable, do not fall back to plaintext files or put credentials into chats, requirements, or delivery files. When the local identity database is unavailable, other local features still work. The recovery entry asks you to type a confirmation text, first creates and verifies a backup, and then resets the local identity data. It is not a reset tool for the whole app's data. Related pages: Collaboration, Runtime & models, Permissions & security.

en.title: Life Science Preview
en.description: View structure, sequence, omics, imaging, and spectral files directly in the workspace.
en.body: Life Science Preview Open a scientific file to see its summary and choose the chain, region, or channel you want to analyze. Life Science Preview is included in SciForge's Biology Workbench. This page covers version 1.1.3 . Open a file Open Files from the toolbar on the far right and select a file in the current workspace. Supported types open in their scientific viewer. Other types open in the regular viewer. A remote workspace reads the preview from the remote file within the workspace's permissions and preview limits. Supported formats and preview content File formats What you can see What to do next --- --- --- .pdb , .cif , .mmcif , .sdf , .mol , .mol2 , .xyz Chain, residue, and ligand summaries and a Mol 3D view Select a region. When coordinates are available, measure distances, angles, or dihedrals. .fasta , .fa , .fna , .faa , .fastq , .gb , .gbk , .gff , .gff3 , .gtf , .bed , .vcf Available record counts, lengths, features, intervals, or variant summaries Select an interval and use its coordinates to read, validate, or analyze the source file. .h5ad , .loom , .mtx , .h5 , .hdf5 , .zarr Available matrix dimensions, observation and variable fields, and names of dimensionality reductions Find the fields you need, then open the full matrix with an appropriate analysis tool. .tif , .tiff , .ome.tif , .ome.tiff , .czi , .svs , .ndpi Dimensions, channels, and OME metadata. Supported TIFF and OME-TIFF files can show thumbnails and regions Select a region of interest (ROI) or channel where available. Use an imaging tool for the pixels in CZI, SVS, or NDPI, or in a compressed or non-8-bit TIFF that only shows file information. .mzml , .mzxml , .mgf , .fcs Available scan or event summaries, peak counts, intensity ranges, and some peak data. FCS mainly shows headers and keywords Annotate a peak interval where available. Use an FCS tool to read the full event matrix. .fai , .gzi , .tbi , .csi An index for an accompanying sequence or genome file Reference the index with its companion data file. Scroll in the preview to see later spectrum, omics, and image summary cards. Use Mol to inspect trajectory or density files. Open the corresponding structure file for chain and residue summaries. Select molecular regions Click a residue in the Mol 3D view to add it. Click the same residue again to remove it, or click empty space to clear the selection. In the selection panel, clicking a chain replaces the selection with that chain. You can also choose a ligand there. The highlights and selection list show the selected chains, residues, atoms, or ligands. Click individual residues one at a time. Use Shift -click for a continuous polymer range. If the list shows a different range than intended, clear the selection and select the residues individually. Selections are stored in the file's preview session. Look at the highlights after reopening a file. When continuing analysis in chat, include the chain and relevant residue or atom IDs in the task. Continue analysis from a preview In the session, specify the file path, region or channel, and the question to analyze. For a remote workspace, use the remote source path. Use the preview to find the relevant part of the file. Use the source file for quantitative analysis, full format validation, or variant detection, and compare the result with the reported inputs and commands. Read limits and exported copies The summary reads the beginning of the file, up to 2 MB (2,000,000 bytes) for text or 4 MiB (4,194,304 bytes) for binary data. When the preview says it is incomplete, its counts cover only the portion it read. Calculate whole-file counts from the source. If a selection is too large, narrow it and try again. To export a copy, open the scientific file from Files on the right. Keep the preview open, and in a session with file-preview tools request a copy in the original format. Provide the source and a new workspace-relative destination. For example, open a FASTA file and request a copy at exports/copy.fasta . Use any available destination that keeps the original format. Opening the preview and reading it require no confirmation. Approve the export after reviewing the source and destination in the write confirmation. Then open the destination folder in Files . The copy appears there with the same file extension. Related pages - Biology Room - Get and organize data - Workbench tools - Feature status and limits

en.title: Features & Extensions overview
en.description: Choose workbench, research analysis, evidence, collaboration, and extension capabilities by the task you want to do.
en.body: Features & Extensions overview Pick the task you want to do from the table below. Built-in features open directly; standalone plugins must be installed; Skills provide working methods; MCP connects external tools. For version information, see Version & Compatibility. Start from your task What you want to do Where to read Current form and conditions --- --- --- Open a project, continue a session, view or edit files Workbench Local workspace, sessions, and file preview for supported formats. When content is too long or a file does not support editing, the page shows the reason. Connect models and executors Runtime & models Codex, Claude Code, and DSH are configured separately. Model access and tool permissions are not the same thing. View sequences, structures, omics, imaging, and spectra Life Science Preview Ships with the app; no separate install needed. Organize biological objects and experiment records Biology Room Ships with the app; used to organize related files and annotations. Plot from data and code, revise, and accept candidates Scientific Figures Needs a compatible plugin installed, plus Python and the required dependencies. Add anchored comments to text or resources Anchored Comments Standalone plugin. Real capture and external feedback each have their own permission requirements. Check what the agent actually changed Change Inspector Plugin you must install. Lets the agent list this session's file differences, and tells you when output is too long. Save artifacts and research evidence Evidence & reproducibility Saves file versions, research stages, and the source of conclusions. Figure records must be linked separately. Run repeated tasks Automation, Create Loop Needs the app running and the matching executor. Multi-step flows and single scheduled instructions are configured separately. Sign in, connect a device, join a project, and deliver tasks Account, Collaboration Local accounts and cloud identity are separate. Team actions also need an available service and role authorization. Use Content Space and notes Content Space, SiYuan Notes You configure the matching service. Server deployment tutorials are not included. Add plugins, working methods, or external tools Extensions & marketplace Check the public catalog and desktop Market for availability, look up bundled extensions, or configure Skills and MCP. Evidence and tool reference - Artifact Versions, Git Checkpoints, Research Checkpoints: fix the state of files or research stages. - Evidence DAG, Project DAG, Research Dossier: organize evidence, project goals, and deliverables. - Terminal, Browser Preview, Computer Use: use external execution capabilities according to the runtime environment and permissions. - Plugin license terms: check licenses and installation requirements. Remote SSH connection and management belong to internal supplements, and the public manual does not provide VPN, SSH target registration, or internal deployment steps. How to tell whether you can use something For installation requirements and current limits, see Feature status.

en.title: Project DAG
en.description: Aggregate project goals, claims, review status, and decisions across sessions.
en.body: Project DAG Project DAG combines the evidence from several sessions in the same project, to help you see which conclusions the project has so far and which questions still need review. First update and save the evidence graph in each session's Evidence DAG, then come back to the project graph and click Update now . After a session saves new evidence, the project graph still has to be updated manually. Opening it - Entry: the Project DAG panel on the right; you can also open the matching view from a project, goal, or historical snapshot. - Target: the project that corresponds to the current workspace, and the evidence graphs each session has saved. - Prerequisite: the project has at least one saved session evidence graph, and the evidence-graph and project-graph features are available. Update and review the project graph 1. Finish the analysis in each session, save the sources and results, and update Evidence DAG for each. Wait until each session's evidence graph has finished saving. 2. Open the Project DAG, fill in the title and description under Project goal , and click Save goal . 3. Click Update now , wait for queueing, execution, and saving to all finish, then check this project graph. Only saving session evidence or closing the panel does not generate a new project graph automatically. 4. Review the items that need attention, the audit status, and the materials provided for review. Select important conclusions and check each one: What does it say? Which sources support it? Can it be traced to the original records? Can the analysis be rerun under its original conditions? What evidence is still missing? 5. When you need to check details, open the matching session's Evidence DAG. After adding sources or results, first save the session evidence graph, then update the project graph manually. When reviewing - Confirm you are reviewing the graph from this update. After a new graph is saved, the old graph's audit results are marked stale, and you should recheck against the current graph. - The audit checks a project graph that is already saved. An audit failure does not undo a graph that was saved, and it does not modify conclusions directly. - Sources you are not allowed to view have their content hidden, and only limited status and gap hints are shown. When reviewing, note which parts could not be checked. - The project graph uses the evidence graphs each session has saved; analysis results that are not yet saved need to be organized in the session first. Saving and sharing Saving a goal and updating the project graph adds project records, so you can review them later. Operations in the panel act on the local project records; publishing or sending content out still needs authorization as the app requires. Before sharing, check source permissions, and state the unverified conclusions and the evidence gaps. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Evidence DAG: save the session evidence the project graph needs. - Research Dossier: turn research results into a readable deliverable. - Workspaces and sessions: how several sessions share one project scope. - Permissions & security: access permissions and publication authorization.

en.title: Research Checkpoints
en.description: Automatically save the summary, sources, and file references of completed research turns, to review and continue later.
en.body: Research Checkpoints Research Checkpoints automatically saves the chat turns that were accepted and completed, recording the research summary, the reasons for changes, the sources, and the related file and Git references. It helps you see what was done at the time, what it was based on, and where to continue next time. The record also hints at which operations were not fully recorded. Opening it - Entry: This turn's research record on a session result card; the card offers Open research dossier . - Target: the completed chat turns in the current session, and the workspace they are bound to. - Prerequisite: automatic recording is on by default and the session is bound to a workspace; the first version is generated after the first turn finishes. View and continue the research 1. Finish a round of research in a session bound to a workspace, and wait for the result card to show that the record has been saved. 2. Look at the title, the reason for changes, and the inputs and outputs, and check whether the sources and related files match this round's work. 3. Look for prompts that an analysis cannot be rerun, or that a result cannot be traced to its sources. When the operation record is incomplete, add the actual commands, environment, and output, so it can be rechecked later. 4. Under Exact artifact versions , choose an output and click Open to check the actual version it references. 5. Click Open research dossier to read the full record; to pick up from a historical record, select it and restore it as a new version, which keeps the existing history. What is saved A checkpoint saves the summary and the references. The actual file contents and artifact versions must be saved and checked separately, see Artifact Versions; for the Git state of the whole workspace, see Git Checkpoints. Having only a research summary does not mean all the result files were kept. Saving adds a checkpoint version based on this turn's conversation, tool results, workspace file changes, and related artifact, computation, and Git records. Existing versions are kept. If the system cannot yet determine where a record should be linked, it is marked pending; check it before continuing. Manage automatic recording In the research dossier, use Turn on automatic recording or Stop automatic recording . Turns completed while recording is stopped are not recorded automatically afterwards. On a version conflict, you can save again based on the current version, or discard this round's record. Importing an old session, handling a conflict, and restoring as a new version need confirmation. Importing an old session keeps only the chat content; the system still warns that the history is incomplete and that some results cannot be traced to sources. The import itself does not fill in the research process that was missing at the time. Tips - Only chat turns that were accepted and completed are recorded; for a task not yet finished, wait until it completes before checking. - Operations done through the terminal, an editor, or similar may be recorded only as what changed, not fully as how those results were produced. Check them against the actual files and run records. - New checkpoints are visible only within the workspace and cannot be exported by default. Before sharing, check access permissions and the record contents. - The record redacts some narrative text, URLs, and credential-like query parameters, but you should still check manually for sensitive information. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Dossier: view records, control automatic recording, and restore historical versions. - Git Checkpoints: save a Git snapshot of the workspace. - Artifact Versions: save the content and versions of related artifacts. - Workspaces and sessions: how a session limits the scope of records.

en.title: Research Dossier
en.description: Turn the research question, inputs, methods, results, and limitations into a readable deliverable.
en.body: Research Dossier The research dossier puts the research summary, sources, key artifacts, versions, and limitations together, for review and delivery. After opening a research record, read the results and the limitations that need attention first, then look at earlier versions as needed. Process records come from Research Checkpoints, and evidence relationships are in Evidence DAG. Opening it - Entry: Research in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown); the right panel is titled Research as well; you can also click Open research dossier on a session result card. - To see history, open a specific artifact version or research record, and first confirm which record you are reading. - Prerequisite: the session is bound to a workspace; after research checkpoints or artifact versions have been saved, you can view the matching detailed records. The research dossier brings the research narrative, version position, credibility summary, and the limitations to consider onto one reading surface. Read and check a record 1. Finish a round of research, and click Open research dossier on the result card. 2. Confirm the selected research record and version, and read the overview, research sources, declared files, and key artifacts. 3. Look at Limitations to consider and Provenance breakpoints , and check item by item the missing sources, unverified results, and reproduction conditions. 4. To review history, load earlier versions in the Versions area, and use Compare exact version to check the differences. 5. When you need an earlier result, choose Restore as new version and confirm, then check the restored result and the actual files. The existing history is kept. When the selected record is missing or fails verification, the dossier shows a prompt. Check the record and the related files, and use it for delivery only after the problem is resolved. Preview and delivery Use Open verified preview to view the selected content, or Export Bundle V2 to package it for delivery. Exporting writes workspace files and asks for confirmation; check that all the required related versions and files are present and allowed to be accessed and exported, and state what has not yet been verified. Before sharing, also check the bundle for sensitive data. Restoring and importing an old session need confirmation as prompted. An imported old session stays marked as having an incomplete history, with the missing provenance information flagged. You can also turn automatic recording on or off here; for its behavior, see Research Checkpoints. Tips - What is shown depends on the checkpoints, artifact versions, and evidence the task has saved. If there are no records yet, finish and save a round of the task first. - When part of the record cannot be read for the moment, the matching content may be unavailable, while the rest of the verified content can still be read. - Empty blocks and inapplicable compute, evidence, or review blocks are omitted. Open Evidence DAG when you need the full evidence relationships. - The summaries and references in the dossier need to be checked against the actual files, especially after the related files were modified, moved, or deleted. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Checkpoints: save the research-process records in the dossier. - Artifact Versions: view, compare, and restore artifact versions. - Evidence DAG: see the complete in-session evidence relationships. - Feature status and limitations: see how far each feature is available.

en.title: Running analysis and computation
en.description: Run analysis in a Python, R, or cluster environment you configured, and keep the inputs, dependencies, and actual outputs.
en.body: Running analysis and computation Before running an analysis, prepare and verify the Python, R, or cluster environment you configured yourself. When you want the Agent to execute, state in the session the environment to use, the input files, the analysis steps, and the output location; which operations are available depends on the execution environment and permissions. 1. Confirm the location, format, and version of the input files, and keep the raw data and source records. 2. Prepare the scripts and the dependencies they need, and record the interpreter, package versions, and run parameters; for cluster jobs, also record the submit command and resource requests. 3. Actually run the analysis, and check the run status, exit code, and logs; on failure, keep the error message, fix it, and run again. 4. Check that the output files and statistical results match expectations, and save how the inputs, code, dependencies, and outputs correspond. Without an actual run record, do not write an expected result up as a completed computation. To plot from data and Python code, revise, and accept candidate figures, use Scientific Figures; that plugin must be installed separately with its dependencies configured, and currently supports Python + Matplotlib. For cross-task source and computation records, see Evidence & reproducibility.

en.title: Scientific Figures
en.description: Select files, describe your plotting request in chat, run Python to generate images, then compare and accept candidate figures.
en.body: Scientific Figures Draw your first line chart from two rows of sample data. Then change its color, compare the candidate with the current chart, and use the run history to find the code and data behind either version. Install and open Scientific Figures 1. Open Extensions → Market and find Scientific Figures . If the entry offers Install , install it and wait for Enabled . If the entry appears under Not installable yet , expand that group to see why. Start at the next step if you have a compatible version enabled. 2. On a macOS system that passes the execution checks, open a writable local workspace and a DSH session with a model configured. Plotting uses Python with Matplotlib installed. If you need to choose the interpreter, set pythonCommand in the plugin configuration. 3. In the right sidebar's plugin picker, choose Scientific Figures (科研图件) . Start when the Figures (图件) tab opens. This guide gives the panel's Chinese button labels alongside their English names. <details <summary Plugin version, platform, and native DSH entry</summary The plugin steps here use 0.4.0-mvp.13 . Native DSH requires =0.2.1-rc.4 <0.3.0 and Node =22. The package includes a native Canvas component. Choose a build that matches your platform, architecture, and Linux libc where applicable. The SciForge plotting entry runs on macOS. Windows and Linux can install compatible packages, while Python execution through this entry requires macOS. Implement plotting steps from R or MATLAB scripts in Python before using this entry. In native DSH, open Figures in the session input area or enter /scientific-figures . </details Select data and code to generate your first figure 1. Save this sample as data/trend.csv in the workspace. csv time,response 0,1.2 1,1.8 2. Open New (新建) → Start from data (从数据开始) and enter data/trend.csv in Data file (数据文件) . Describe the chart you want. You can adapt this example: text Read data/trend.csv. Draw a blue line chart with time on the x-axis and response on the y-axis. Use the column names as labels because the data has no units. Save the data and code, run it, and publish the PNG. 3. Click Start plotting (开始绘图) . When the session shows a result, return to Figures , click Refresh (刷新) , and select the new figure. The line should run from (0, 1.2) to (1, 1.8). For an existing script, select Existing data and code (已有数据和代码) and enter the workspace-relative paths to the data and Python script. You can add an original image for comparison. The panel labels it as user-provided and unverified, and saves the PNG from the new run separately. Find images, code, and run results Select a chart in Figures and expand All versions and sources (所有版本与来源) to see the code version and run behind it. Open Code and runs (代码与运行) , select the run, and click Read run (读取运行) to view its inputs, parameters, environment, and logs. The code and run lists each show 20 summaries per page. Click More code versions (更多代码版本) or More run records (更多运行记录) to open the next page. Each code version saves a copy of its data, the parameters, and the source version. To rerun it, load that version and use the saved inputs. To use updated workspace files, select Read workspace data again (重新读取工作区数据) in the advanced settings and save a new version. Revise a figure, compare it, then accept 1. In Figures , select the sample chart, describe a change in the request box, and click Send to AI (发送给 AI) —for example, keeping the data and making the line orange. After the new run finishes, click Refresh (刷新) . The orange line appears as a candidate. 2. Compare Current (当前图) and Revised (修改后) . Use Candidate (候选) to switch between results when several are available. 3. Click Request acceptance (申请接受) and open the approval prompt in the left session. Click Allow (允许) , then return to Figures and click Refresh . The orange line becomes Current (当前图) , while the previous figure and its code stay in the history. Click Keep current (保留当前图) to retain the current figure instead. If the current figure changed after the candidate was generated, select the current figure and generate a new candidate from that version. Analysis files, history, and recovery Use analysis outputs in the next step. In the script, write intermediate results such as cleaned.csv , summary.json , or rules.txt to SCIENTIFIC_FIGURES_OUTPUT_DIR . In Code and runs , select the run and click Read run . The Output files (输出文件) dropdown lists each path and its size in bytes. Select a file to see its SHA-256 digest below the list. In the session, specify the run and file you want to reuse, or enter the path manually as shown below. After saving a new code version, expand Version and input snapshot (版本与输入快照) to see the copied input. <details <summary Manual input paths and output limits</summary Open Code and runs → Advanced settings: parameters, inputs, and files (高级设置：参数、输入与文件) . If you are starting from a parent version, select Read workspace data again (重新读取工作区数据) . Prefix the relative path shown in Output files (the tool's output.path ) with .scientific-figures/ . Enter it in Workspace input paths JSON (工作区输入路径 JSON) , for example [".scientific-figures/path-from-the-run/cleaned.csv"] . This field sets inputPaths . Click Save and freeze code (保存并冻结代码) and expand Version and input snapshot to see the saved copy. Output Format Limit per run --- --- --- Publish as a figure or candidate PNG 16 files, 20 MiB each, 64 MiB total Reuse in analysis Valid UTF-8 CSV, TSV, or TXT, or parseable JSON 32 files, 8 MiB each, 32 MiB total If saving fails, open the run and use the error message to adjust the file format, size, or count before rerunning. </details Complete an interrupted save. If saving stopped after Python finished, open Code and runs → Unfinished or interrupted runs (尚未结束或中断的运行) and click Complete interrupted record (完成中断记录) on that run. Once completed, the record moves to the run history with its original logs and outputs. If the panel reports missing results, an unconfirmed process state, or a busy record, resolve that issue first. For a failed run, read the error log in the run details, fix the code or environment, and rerun from Run frozen Python (执行已冻结 Python) . Other history entries and pages remain accessible if a single record is damaged. View code and run it manually 1. In Code and runs , select a version and click Load version (载入版本) . After editing it, click Save and freeze code (保存并冻结代码) . The new version appears in the Version (版本) list. 2. Click Run frozen Python (执行已冻结 Python) . The run details display the status, exit code, inputs, parameters, and output files. Expand the code comparison, environment, or logs if you need to investigate. 3. After a successful run, select a PNG in Output files and choose where to publish it. - New figure. Click Publish as a new figure (发布为新图件文档) . Return to Figures and click Refresh . The new figure appears in the Figures (图件) dropdown. - Candidate for an existing figure. Select Publish as a candidate for an existing document (发布为现有文档的候选图) and choose its Target document (目标文档) . Click Read and select current baseline (读取并选定当前基线) . When Explicit baseline (明确基线) appears, click Publish as candidate (发布为候选图) . Return to Figures , click Refresh , and open the target figure’s Candidate (候选) menu. Rebuild the environment from the saved instructions In Code and runs , load a successful run and use the output path to locate its _environment/ directory: - environment.json : records the Python version, operating system, and dependencies from the original run so you can compare environments. - requirements.txt : pins the Python packages to the exact versions recorded during the run. - REBUILD.md : gives step-by-step instructions to create an isolated environment and install dependencies before rerunning. Prepare system libraries and drivers on the target machine separately. After changing the operating system or Python version, run the saved code with its saved inputs and compare the generated output files and key values. Troubleshooting What you see Next step --- --- The session has a result, but the panel shows an earlier figure Click Refresh (刷新) , then select the figure and candidate from this run. The plotting request failed to send Keep your input. Check the DSH connection in Settings → AI assistant . Check model access in Settings → General . When both are ready, retry in the DSH session. Python or Matplotlib cannot be found Open the run log in Code and runs , then fix the pythonCommand path or install Matplotlib in that interpreter before rerunning. The session attachment says File not found Click Read run (读取运行) again in Code and runs , check whether the PNG appears under Output files , and check the plugin version. The candidate did not become the current figure Open the approval prompt in the session and click Allow , then return to Figures and click Refresh . If the current figure changed, select the new current figure and generate a candidate from it. The code failed to execute Open the standard error log in Code and runs , fix the script, click Save and freeze code and Run frozen Python , and publish after the status shows completed . Current scope and limits Figure data is saved in the workspace's .scientific-figures/ directory. To include the figure in a research record, keep its data, code, and results. See Evidence and reproducibility. Start in a writable workspace outside the system's temporary directory, with execution isolation enabled. The workspace used when the session starts defines the write scope. Python may still read other files or access the network, so run code you trust. Check the model provider's data policy before sending plotting data. Related pages - Scientific Figures cases - Extension Center - Runtime and models - Workspaces and sessions - Feature status and limits - Versions and compatibility

en.title: SiYuan Notes
en.description: Connect your own SiYuan service to the workbench and archive traceable Markdown summaries after tasks finish.
en.body: SiYuan Notes Open your SiYuan service from SciForge to read or update research notes, or save a session result to a specific document. How to open it 1. Prepare a reachable HTTP or HTTPS SiYuan service in server mode. You can use a service you deploy or subscribe to. Have the API Token ready if the service requires one. 2. Click SiYuan Notes (labeled Cloud Services in some builds) in the left sidebar. In its Settings , enter the Service address and click Save settings . Leaving it blank uses the installation's default address. Enter the API token in Settings or set SIYUAN_API_TOKEN in the launch environment. The token from Settings takes precedence and is stored in the app's encrypted storage. 3. Once the editor opens, choose the notebook and document. You can also click Test saved connection in Settings to see a read-verified connection status before editing. For a connection error, click Retry or return to Settings to check the address and token. The editor opens to the right of the session. You can move it from the header to the left, bottom, or main area and resize it. The app saves its position and size on this device. Open an existing note Open SiYuan Notes from the left sidebar, then choose the notebook and document. Reopen the document after editing to see the saved text. To find material from a session, ask the assistant to search by title or path fragment, then give the resulting document ID or path to read the Markdown body. If the result is marked as truncated, specify the section you need. Content Space can locate open SiYuan notebooks. Use the SiYuan editor or session tools to work with a document. Save a session result to SiYuan Specify the notebook, path, title, and content in the session. As an example you can adapt, ask the session to save this turn's QC summary as “Weekly QA” in the “Project A” notebook under /Sample QC . After the write completes, open that location in SiYuan Notes ; the document body should contain the QC summary. View automatic archives A successful top-level agent turn with a final reply is archived automatically to the connected SiYuan service. Decide which content can be sent to that service before starting. After the task finishes, open the SciForge 工作总结 notebook in SiYuan Notes and find the turn by timestamp under /SciForge . The archived document contains the prompt, the final reply, the completion timestamp, and the turn ID. The first archive creates the SciForge 工作总结 notebook if it does not exist yet. To save an intermediate result during a task, specify a destination document in the session. If SciForge can’t reach the service or verify that the write finished, it keeps the pending document on this device. It retries when the app next starts or the next top-level turn finishes. Before writing, it looks for a document from the same turn to avoid duplicates. Once the service is back, open /SciForge in its SciForge 工作总结 notebook to find the archived document. Related pages - Content Space - Collaboration guide - Permissions and security - Feature status and limits Component version: @sciforge/domain-siyuan-content-space-provider v0.3.1.

en.title: Terminal
en.description: Run commands directly in the workspace, verify the results, and keep key output in the session.
en.body: Terminal Terminal puts the command-line environment for the current workspace in the bottom panel. It is suited to running scripts, checking logs, and confirming the status of long-running tasks. You type commands in the panel yourself; when the Agent runs commands in a session, it follows the Runtime's approval and sandbox policies. The permission settings for the two apply separately. How to open it - Entry: Terminal in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown), or Terminal in the bottom panel. - Target: the current workspace. The terminal process uses the workspace root as its initial working directory. - Prerequisite: a workspace is open, and the local or remote Workspace Host can start a system shell. - Tabs: a workspace can have multiple tabs (up to 8), with support for renaming, closing other tabs, closing all tabs, and restarting the process. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Run a one-off command Enter a command in a tab and press Enter Terminal output and the process exit status Watch a long-running task Keep the tab open and scroll through the ongoing output Task progress; closing the tab ends that terminal process Separate tasks Create and name separate tabs Command-line sessions isolated by tab Reproduce experiment steps Put the commands in a script, run it in the terminal, and record key output Commands you can run again, plus exit statuses Typical workflow 1. Confirm that the workspace shown at the top is the project this task should work on. 2. Open Terminal and run pwd and read-only commands first to confirm the directory, interpreter, and dependencies. 3. For commands that will write files, access the network, or install software, check the target paths, arguments, and recovery plan first. 4. Explain the purpose of the command in the session, and bring key output, exit statuses, or error messages back into the conversation. 5. Check the file state after the task. Copy terminal content you need to keep into notes or an artifact. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: commands can read files, environment variables, and network resources that the current user has permission to access. - Writes: commands can modify workspace files and may also write outside the workspace. The working directory is not a filesystem sandbox. - Approval or external effects: Terminal does not prompt for each command. Operations such as installing dependencies, accessing the network, and overwriting files take effect directly under the current user's permissions. - Agent execution: commands started by the Agent are governed by its Runtime's approval and sandbox settings. There is no promise that all commands skip approval, and no guarantee that every command triggers a prompt. - Output retention: commands and output stay with the tab in the current workspace and are not kept after the tab closes. Results from Agent-started commands return to the session context with the tool call. - What it does not do: it does not automatically write terminal content into the conversation record. Closing a tab ends the corresponding terminal process, but switching workspaces does not automatically end terminals that are already running. Known limitations - Terminal processes in remote workspaces run remotely, and output is read through incremental cursors. Remote controlled terminals are pipe-based and do not claim full pseudo-terminal (PTY) compatibility. - The tab limit is 8. Closing all tabs collapses the panel, and unsaved screen content is not restored. - Command availability depends on the shell, PATH, and dependencies on the local or remote host. SciForge does not install missing tools for you. - Terminal scrollback is limited. Write important output to files or logs, and use persistent scheduling or logging for long-running tasks. - Content in the manual terminal does not automatically enter the Agent context. To inform the Agent, paste the necessary excerpts into the session or have it run the commands itself. Related pages - Workbench tools: how files, Terminal, Browser, and Computer Use divide responsibilities. - Workspaces and sessions: workspace locations and session state. - Permissions and security: approvals, credentials, and the scope of command effects. - Remote resources and collaboration: terminals and data boundaries in remote workspaces. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-terminal v1.0.1.

en.title: View and revise figures
en.description: Describe figure changes in words, then compare and accept the candidate after it actually runs.
en.body: View and revise figures Use the standalone Scientific Figures plugin to generate figures from data and Python + Matplotlib code. Install a compatible plugin and prepare the environment it needs first, then state the plotting or revision request in words. 1. Choose the data and code in the workspace, and say what to change, for example "keep the data, make the line blue, and shorten the title". With only an image, the exact data cannot be recovered. 2. Have the Agent save a new code version and actually run it, check the run status and the output, and generate a candidate figure once it succeeds. 3. Compare the current version and the candidate under Current figure / After change ; when there are several candidates, switch among them in the Candidates drop-down. 4. When satisfied, click Request acceptance , then go to the session, check the figure, and click Allow to make the candidate the current figure; to keep revising, state the next request. The plugin keeps immutable code, input, run, and image versions; accepting a candidate updates the current figure, while the original figure and the run records are kept. After a figure changes, a candidate may need to be regenerated. It has no on-image boxes, arrows, or pins for annotation, and it does not register records with artifact versions or evidence relationships automatically. To leave feedback on specific text, use the standalone Anchored Comments. When you need a screenshot, enable that feature first. A comment only records feedback; changing the image still requires running the plot again and accepting the candidate. For organizing and delivering results, see Evidence & reproducibility.

en.title: Five-minute quickstart
en.description: Open a local project, analyze it read-only with Codex, and verify the file state before and after the task.
en.body: Five-minute quickstart Start by having the Agent examine a local project in read-only mode: open a workspace, confirm Codex's permissions, send a task, then compare the file state. When you are done, you should see a project overview and no changes to project files. 1. Prepare a project and a model Start SciForge, prepare a clean Git project or a copy of a project, and configure working model access and Codex. For the first run you can start from a local workspace without signing in to the collaboration cloud. In the first-run wizard or Settings → General , choose Model API or Coding Plan . Then go to Settings → AI assistant and check whether Codex is detected. Settings is at the bottom of the expanded left sidebar; account and cloud status are in the same area. Illustrates the two paths, Model API and Coding Plan. 2. Record the file state and set read-only permissions Run this in the project directory and save the output: bash git status --short If there are already modifications, record them clearly first; for a non-Git project, use a copy. Go to Settings → AI assistant → Codex and set File access range to Can only read files , keeping an appropriate tool approval policy. Wait for the setting to apply, finish any existing tasks, then reconnect or restart and start a new session. “Can edit workspace” in the figure allows writes; change it to “Can only read files” before starting this tutorial. For detailed steps, see configure a read-only sandbox. Write the no-modification instruction into the prompt as well; if you see a request to widen permissions, stop and check, because this task needs no write access. 3. Open a local workspace and start a new session In the Workspace location menu, choose Local workspace, open the project directory, and check the path and the project name on the left. Start a new session, and confirm in the bottom input area that the execution runtime is Codex . The left side of the current workbench is for project, session, and collaboration navigation; the vertical toolbar on the far right opens tools such as files, and panels dock beside it. If there are many tools, open More tools . Shows a local project and a new session. 4. Send your first task Enter: Look at the current workspace, list only the top-level files and directories, and describe in one sentence what this project might be. Do not modify files or install dependencies. For this read-only trial, use Files or type @ if you need to reference a file already in the workspace. Importing a file from outside the workspace saves a copy there. Try that in a later task. For the difference between the attachment tray and the labels on sent files, see workspaces and sessions. Shows the task text and the execution runtime. After sending, watch the tool calls, working directory, and execution results in the session. If the Runtime is not connected, check Settings → AI assistant and the model configuration first, then send again. Shows the execution state within the same session. 5. Verify the results and files The answer should list the top-level contents and give a grounded judgment about what the project is. Run again: bash git status --short Compare with the pre-task state and confirm that no project files were added, deleted, or modified. Git does not show ignored caches; when you need a strict check, also compare your copy's file list and content hashes. If you find changes, stop and investigate rather than restoring existing modifications outright. Viewing the analysis result in the session. Once you confirm that the workspace is correct, Codex responds normally, read-only permissions are applied, and the file state matches the pre-task state, you have completed your first task. Next, you can continue with: Continue the read-only analysis. Explain what the main directories are for, the likely entry files, and a recommended way to start or test the project. List anything that cannot be confirmed from the source separately. Do not modify files or install dependencies. Continue reading: Runtime and model access, working with the Agent.

en.title: Configure a read-only sandbox
en.description: Configure Codex's read-only execution scope, understand how Claude Plan mode differs, and compare Git status before and after a task.
en.body: Configure a read-only sandbox “Do not modify files” in a prompt is a task requirement; you also need to configure execution permissions. This page uses the Codex read-only sandbox as the getting-started path; the file-scope option of the same name in Claude Code corresponds to Plan mode , and these modes enforce different restrictions. Where the setting lives 1. Expand the left sidebar and open Settings from the bottom. 2. Go to AI assistant . 3. In the AI assistant configuration cards at the top of the page, find Codex . 4. Find the File access range dropdown under that Runtime and select Can only read files . 5. Wait for the setting to apply, then reconnect or restart SciForge after finishing the current task; do not keep using a running task whose permissions are not yet confirmed. 6. Return to the workbench, start a new session, and confirm in the bottom-right of the input box that the execution runtime is codex . The Access shortcut at the top of the page jumps to the Computer Use configuration; the file access range is in each Runtime's own configuration section. The value shown allows workspace changes; select “Can only read files” for read-only tasks. Runtime What “Can only read files” actually means Boundaries --- --- --- Codex Requests Codex's readOnly sandbox and disables command network access within that sandbox Suitable for the local file inspection in this tutorial; stop and check any request that widens permissions Claude Code Uses Claude Code's plan permission mode For analysis and planning; do not claim it provides the same filesystem sandbox isolation as Codex DSH Has no file access range option of the same name; the native shell is off by default and, once enabled for a DSH you installed, approved command by command This tutorial uses Codex; do not treat DSH's shell switch as a filesystem read-only sandbox MCP, remote commands, and Computer Use permissions must each be checked separately; for your first task, use only the tools needed to read the local project. Adding files from outside the workspace, dragging files in, or pasting images may import files into the workspace first. For a read-only check, reference existing files and record the baseline again once the import completes. Removing an attachment above the input box only cancels this send; it does not delete files that have already been imported. What read-only mode allows You can usually: - List directories and read text files - Search source and configuration - View Git status and diffs - Run checks that do not write to the workspace - Provide analyses, plans, and recommendations You should not allow: - Creating, overwriting, renaming, or deleting files - Installing dependencies that write to the project - Running commands that generate caches, logs, or build artifacts - Modifying the Git index, commits, or branches Whether a command is truly read-only depends on what it does, not what it is called. Some tests and interpreters generate caches automatically; if you hit a write failure in the read-only sandbox, change your checking approach rather than widening permissions just to finish the tutorial. Double verification In a Git project, run this before and after the task: bash git status --short Comparing Git status detects changes but does not replace execution isolation; it also does not list files ignored by .gitignore . When you need a strict check of every file, use a copy of the project and additionally compare the file list and content hashes before and after the task. If the output changes: 1. Stop any further tasks immediately. 2. Have the Agent list the changes, and check the file differences with git diff . 3. Do not automatically delete or restore existing modifications. 4. Determine whether the changes come from the task, from tool caches, or already existed before the task. When to switch to workspace write Switch to Can edit workspace only when a task explicitly needs to generate scripts, tables, figures, or documents and you have checked the plan and output paths. Write tasks should use a project copy or a clean branch, and you should review the changes when finished. Next: working with the Agent.

en.title: Runtime and model access
en.description: Configure model access, choose Codex, Claude Code, or DeepSeek Harness, and complete a connection check.
en.body: Runtime and model access Configure the model service first, then choose the AI assistant that executes tasks. The former determines where model requests go; the latter plans work and calls tools. Setting Entry point What to confirm --- --- --- Model access First-run wizard or Settings → General The Model API base URL, key, and model, or official sign-in for Coding Plan AI assistant Settings → AI assistant Installation, connection, and permissions for Codex, Claude Code, or DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Current session Execution settings in the bottom input area The Runtime, model, and available tiers for this run Settings is at the bottom of the expanded left sidebar. Local accounts and SciForge cloud sign-in are managed separately, see Identity & Access. Choose model access With Model API , enter the Base URL, API Key, and model name provided by your service provider; if you are unsure about the protocol, use automatic detection. An existing key only means the field is configured; whether the upstream accepts it must be confirmed with an actual request. This screenshot illustrates the configuration fields. Enter your own service settings. With Coding Plan , complete official sign-in or device-code authorization in the interface. The Coding Plan path currently supports Codex; Claude Code uses model access. If sign-in or connection fails, fix the current access path according to the prompt, then retry. Choose and connect a Runtime In Settings → AI assistant , choose the execution runtime and check the detection result; if automatic detection fails, use Choose local app or enter the absolute path to the executable, then detect again. - Codex : uses the installed Codex app-server; check the model and permissions before starting a task. - Claude Code : configure model access and check its permission mode. - DSH : connects through a local ACP program; the model and reasoning tier take effect in the session after connecting. Check the program you specified, the system path, and common install locations first, and only try the component bundled with the app when none of them work. DSH's Shell command execution is off by default; enable it only for a DSH you installed yourself, and each run still requires approval. Do not switch to full permissions just to make an error go away. Shows execution runtime configuration, tool confirmations, and file scope. Codex and Claude Code can edit the workspace by default. For your first analysis, adjust permissions according to configure a read-only sandbox first. After switching execution runtimes, re-check the connection, sign-in, and permissions; existing sessions' mappings and configuration do not migrate automatically. When you need to operate desktop applications, also check Computer Use 's Runtime support, backend, and system permissions. Illustrates the configuration items that must be checked separately. Run a minimal connection check Start a new session, confirm that the expected Runtime is selected in the input area, and send: Reply only with “connected”. Do not read or modify files, and do not call external services. After you receive a response, continue to the five-minute quickstart. If the selected Runtime is unavailable, fix it according to the error or switch deliberately; the app will not automatically pick another Runtime for you. Troubleshoot DSH timeouts DSH distinguishes between a timeout on a single connection request and a task that makes no progress for a long time: Case Meaning and handling --- --- Initialization, create, or resume session requests time out The default single wait is 15 seconds. Check the local program, the connection, and any explicit error; extending the wait will not solve long-running tasks A task produces no session updates for a long time By default, the turn stops after 10 minutes of continuous silence; long tasks that keep receiving updates for the current session can exceed 10 minutes. Review the existing results before deciding whether to continue the same session For technical troubleshooting: the former's configuration name is requestTimeoutMs ; the latter, although named promptTimeoutMs , means the idle limit and has the error code runtime_prompt_idle_timeout . After a timeout, the original session identifier can be recovered, but you should still check existing files and external actions before continuing the task.

en.title: SciForge User Manual
en.description: From opening a project and handing the AI a task to checking results, saving records, and collaborating with your team.
en.body: SciForge User Manual In SciForge, you can open a project, let the AI read materials, modify files, run analyses, and create figures, then check the results and request changes. The files, conversations, and run records from a task remain available for review and for later collaboration. If this is your first time, start with the five-minute quickstart. If you already have a specific question, use the outline below to find the right page; there is no need to read the whole manual from beginning to end. The manual has six parts Part When to read it What it covers --- --- --- Getting started The first time you open SciForge Connect a model, choose an execution runtime, open a project, and complete a simple task; set read-only access or allow file changes. Workbench guides You want to know where a button is or how to hand files to the AI Workspaces and sessions, adding attachments, file preview, panel layout, Terminal and Browser Preview, as well as how to describe a task and check results. Features & Extensions You need to complete a particular kind of research work Scientific file preview, plotting and comments, versions and research records, team collaboration, notes, scheduled tasks, and extensions. Case tutorials You want to see how a complete task is done From input data through running an analysis, revising results, and delivering them; includes scientific plotting, multi-person RNA-seq collaboration, and virtual cell cases. Settings & security You need to adjust file access, tool permissions, or connected services File and network access, action confirmations, and the conditions for using remote resources and team collaboration. Reference & troubleshooting You hit an error or a version mismatch, or need to look up installation requirements Troubleshooting, versions and compatibility, feature limits, and extension licenses. Find a page by goal - Have the AI read a project first : five-minute quickstart. - Hand files to the AI and continue an earlier conversation : workspaces and sessions. - Open a sequence, molecular structure, or omics file : Life Science Preview. - Plot from data, then refine step by step : Scientific Figures. - See which files changed and save intermediate results : Evidence & Reproducibility. - Invite members, assign tasks, and review deliverables : team collaboration. - Install extensions or connect external tools : extensions and marketplace. - The interface does not match the tutorial : versions and compatibility. A few names to start with Name Meaning --- --- Workspace The project directory you open, which holds the files a task uses. Session A conversation around one task, which you can come back to and continue at any time. Runtime (execution runtime) The program that handles tasks; you can choose Codex, Claude Code, or DSH. For configuration, see Runtime and model access. Research records Keep intermediate results, the run process, and the basis for conclusions, so you can look them up and continue later.

en.title: Documentation maintenance checklist
en.description: Maintain one user manual against the latest client, and check versions, links, and the public boundary.
en.body: Documentation maintenance checklist User tutorials are maintained only in sciforge-docs-v2 . The client repository keeps the site entry points, install and development notes, and internal supplements; it no longer duplicates the full tutorials. 1. Pin this round's version Record the date and commit of the latest client mainline first, then verify the interfaces, settings, package versions, and operations the change touches. Update Version and compatibility and the repository README. Record the public source commit separately; do not wait for it to update before writing the manual. Read the current implementation, not just the old README, test names, or planning documents. If a behavior exists only as a test expectation and is not wired into any actual call, list it as an item to verify; do not write it up as an operating step. 2. Update content and navigation - Write "where to open it, how to operate it, what you get" first, then the limits that affect the operation. - Use the actual names shown in the interface. Do not repeat the mainline commit, permission terms, and verification notes on every page; link to the version page instead. - When a feature moves, adjust the overview, sidebar, and related links. Keep a short migration note at the old URL and take it out of the current feature navigation. - English site: update the same-path pages under i18n/en/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/ . When you add or remove a page or rename a sidebar category, also update i18n/en/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current.json . - Do not claim "all plugins are available" from a directory count. Describe built-in modules, standalone plugins, Skills, and MCP separately. - Keep the original date and version on screenshots and cases. Do not relabel them as a new-version demo unless re-recorded; add one sentence to outdated screens. 3. Check the public boundary The public site may describe user operations of the latest client. Internal deployment, database migration, VPN/SSH management, server-side adaptation, real account configuration, and private acceptance material stay in internal documents. General usage such as client sign-in, device connection, and team projects can be public. For new images, first check for visible accounts, paths, tokens, and rights to the material. Keep already-reviewed images; do not bulk-restore old media from the private repository. Keep plugin licenses, original-author attribution, and third-party notices as they are; documentation updates do not change licenses or repository visibility. 4. Keep entry points consistent The user-manual links on the public and private client home pages both point to https://agi4sci.github.io/sciforge-docs-v2/ . Old manual pages inside the repository keep a link to the matching site page. Internal supplements do not go into the public export. Later source exports must keep the licenses, replacement assets, security test fixtures, and these entry points that the public repository has already reviewed; do not overwrite the public repository with the private repository's directories. 5. Build and check bash npm ci npm run typecheck npm run build The build generates the search index and checks internal links. Also check whether retired features still appear on the home page, sidebar, search suggestions, and video chapter descriptions. A successful build only shows the docs can be built; the content still needs a page-by-page review. If the video is not re-recorded, keep the original file and chapter order, and note the applicable version on the guide page. When chapter data is involved, also run node scripts/check-tour.cjs . 6. Publish and spot-check Review through a PR, and wait for the GitHub Pages deployment to succeed after merging. Spot-check the home page, the version page, the feature overview, and this round's key pages online, and confirm the new content and page links work. The PR should state the basis for the update, the main pages, the check results, and any screenshots that need to be retaken later. If something goes wrong, roll back with a new revert PR; do not deploy an earlier site configuration.

en.title: Remote resources and collaboration
en.description: Distinguish remote workspace sessions from SciForge Cloud collaboration, and understand the data and permission boundaries of each.
en.body: Remote resources and collaboration Remote workspaces address "where compute and data live"; Cloud collaboration addresses "who works together around a Project and Task." The two can be combined or used independently. Remote workspaces A remote workspace brings a SciForge Workspace Host session running on another machine into the local workbench: files, terminals, Git, and Agent requests act on the remote directory, while the interface stays on your machine. - Entry point: the Workspace location selector at the top of the workbench, which switches between Local workspace and attached remote sessions; the selector also shows each remote session's lifecycle (Persistent server / Connection session), connection status (Remote, Reconnecting, Offline, Limited, Connection error), and network exit. - When a session disconnects or errors, use Reconnect on the target session in the selector. - The open-source client does not include a connection management panel for registering SSH targets, VPN environments, and workspace authorization; remote sessions appear in the selector only after the deployer provides and attaches them. Before running a command, use Workspace location to identify the remote connection and its path. Files, terminals, and agent commands act on that remote directory. After connecting, check the remote path and file reads first, then test the terminal and the tools you need. If one tool reports that it is unavailable, do not conclude that the entire remote workspace is unusable; for the specific scope, see Version and compatibility. Cloud collaboration Use Cloud collaboration when you need to continue a personal Session on your phone, or when a team needs to assign and accept Tasks around a Project. It requires the Cloud service address, account, and collaboration service configuration provided by your administrator. For team procedures, see Collaboration guide; for a real submission, revision, and downstream handoff, see Pasilla three-person collaboration case. Check the sign-in and device prerequisites for team collaboration in that guide; setting up a personal Session on your phone is a separate path. Figure 2: Cloud connection status and the local workspace are independent of each other. Unified sign-in has three distinct states: State Purpose --- --- Local account Marks the current user and ownership on this machine Cloud sign-in Confirms your cloud identity Device connection Click Connect this device to authorize the current desktop installation to access Cloud capabilities A local account is not cloud authentication; a connected workspace also does not mean you have joined a collaboration Project. In collaboration, Shared files is for viewing resources provided by the content service; there is currently no direct upload entry point. Task delivery follows the Task submission and acceptance process; do not treat the Shared files entry as a general-purpose cloud drive upload. Figure 3: Team collaboration revolves around Projects, Tasks, owners, and acceptance results. Data and credential boundaries - SSH keys, VPN credentials, and MFA are managed by the user or by system security infrastructure. - Cloud, collaboration services, and Content Space may send data to external services. - Before uploading production data, confirm the destination, scope, retention policy, and team permissions. - Remote commands and collaborative tasks should still record inputs, outputs, return codes, and approvals. - After a network interruption, confirm the state of the remote process before deciding whether to retry, to avoid submitting compute twice. Case: Virtual cell perturbation prediction benchmark.

en.title: Permissions and security
en.description: Choose read-only, workspace write, approval, and Computer Use permissions according to the impact of the task.
en.body: Permissions and security First choose the file access range for the task, then check the terminal, plugin, remote service, and computer-use permissions you will use. Confirm the workspace and output locations before running, and verify the destination before submitting or uploading. File access range Range Suitable tasks Main risks --- --- --- Can only read files Project understanding, code review, data inventory, and planning Codex uses a read-only sandbox; Claude uses Plan mode, and the two are not equivalent Can edit workspace Modifying code and generating analyses, figures, and reports Overwriting existing files, writing to the wrong directory, and mixing in unrelated changes Can access all files Controlled tasks that explicitly require cross-directory reads or writes Removes read-only or workspace scope limits and runs tools automatically, potentially affecting data and configuration outside the workspace For a first task, an unfamiliar repository, or an unreviewed Skill, start with the Codex read-only configuration. Both Codex and Claude allow workspace writes in their initial configuration, so you must change this deliberately; MCP, remote execution, and Computer Use each require separate permission checks. For details, see Configuring a read-only sandbox. Approval policy An approval request should state at least: - What operation will be performed - The target files, directories, hosts, or external services - Whether it will write, upload, send, or delete - Whether it can be retried safely after a failure - How to check the result and recover The absence of an approval dialog does not mean an operation is read-only. Manual terminals run with the current system user's permissions; plugins must also be installed, enabled, and granted permissions for the relevant version separately. Credentials - Do not put API keys, tokens, or passwords in prompts, Git repositories, or screenshots. - MCP, the Model API, and collaboration services should each use the minimum credential scope they need. - Do not treat a provider key as a Runtime login credential. - Before exporting logs, traces, or a research dossier, check for Authorization headers, server addresses, real paths, and sample privacy. Computer Use Computer Use can operate supported web pages and in-app embedded pages. Before using it, check the run status in SciForge settings; macOS users also need to check the Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions. Figure 1: Before enabling it, check the chosen executor, the run status, and the system permissions. The following actions should be confirmed by the user at the moment they are performed: account sign-in or authorization, sending messages, uploading data, purchasing or paying, deleting external content, and submitting formal evaluation results. When Scientific Figures accepts a candidate figure, it requires a formal tool call in the session and host confirmation; "Request acceptance" in the panel only initiates the request. Deleting anchored comments and submitting feedback also have their own confirmation steps; see the corresponding feature pages for details. Research data security - Use public or redistributable data for tutorials. - Do not overwrite raw data by default; write derived results to a separate directory. - Whether data in a remote workspace may be downloaded is determined by the project policy. - External models, MCP, and web uploads change the data boundary and must be evaluated separately. - Screenshots should hide real account names, keys, patient information, and server details. Pre-task checklist - [ ] The workspace or project copy is correct - [ ] A Git baseline has been recorded - [ ] The Runtime and file access range match the task - [ ] Output directories and overwrite policy are clear - [ ] Boundaries for network, installation, sign-in, and upload are clear - [ ] Acceptance and recovery methods are clear

en.title: Feature status and limitations
en.description: See the conditions for using each feature and its current limits.
en.body: Feature status and limitations The table below lists the conditions for using each feature and its current limits. Capability Conditions Current scope and limits --- --- --- Workspace, sessions, and workbench layout Built in Common tools are on the right, and the account entry is below the left sidebar. Codex / Claude Code Built in Choose the executor to use, then connect a model and set file and tool permissions. DSH Runtime Built in A task can run for a long time while it keeps reporting progress; when there is no response for a long time, check the connection and continue the original session. Attachments and file references after sending Built in Selected, dragged, or pasted files enter the attachment tray; file references are kept after sending. State in the task which file to read and what to check. Preview of text, code, and other files Built in Some files can be edited directly; when one cannot be edited, the page shows the reason. Local account, cloud device, and usage Built in Deleting a local account does not delete a cloud account or user files; cloud and model-provider identities are managed separately. Team collaboration Needs the service and project permissions Entries for Board, Members, Requirements, Shared files, and Project info; shared files come from task deliveries, and there is currently no direct upload. For the full walkthrough, see the Pasilla case. Biology Workbench preview Built in Large files may show only a summary; after changing a molecular selection, reopen to check it. Scientific Figures Needs the plugin Saves plotting data, code, run results, and images. Needs Python and Matplotlib; R is not supported yet. Anchored Comments Needs the plugin Select text to save a comment; screenshots need the matching feature enabled, and deleting and submitting feedback need confirmation. Change Inspector Needs the plugin Have the Agent list this session's file differences, and page through them when too long. Artifact versions, checkpoints, Evidence / Project DAG, and dossier Configured per feature Save file versions and research records, and see the basis for conclusions in the evidence graph and the project graph. Scheduled tasks and Create Loop Needs the app running Set up repeating tasks or multi-step flows; operations that need confirmation pause and wait. Plugin marketplace, Skills, MCP Configured by type The current public source build’s desktop Market lists no installable plugins. Configure Skills and MCP separately. Remote SSH management Internal supplement The public site does not provide VPN, SSH target registration, or server-side operation steps. Virtual cell models, Slurm/PBS/Kubernetes scheduling Connect your own Use the model or cluster environment you configured yourself. When reporting a problem, include the system, the client and plugin versions, the steps taken, and a screenshot.
